blocks.h: 1. Why the hull form governs the power a ship needs

blocks.p: The power delivered to the propeller is the ship's resistance multiplied by her speed and divided by the propulsive coefficient. Hull form acts on both terms, which is why it is the largest single design lever on lifetime fuel consumption. Resistance divides into a frictional component, which scales with wetted surface and dominates at low speed; a wave-making component, which rises very steeply with speed-length ratio; and a viscous pressure component associated with the boundary layer and flow separation aft. Form controls the wave and pressure components directly, and it controls the propulsive coefficient indirectly through the flow it delivers to the propeller.

Two consequences follow, and they set up the whole answer. First, the hull is a single, irreversible decision: it is fixed at the design stage and, unlike an engine setting or a maintenance interval, it cannot be adjusted afterwards without cutting steel. Second, the two ends of the ship are solving completely different problems. Forward, the hull is fighting the water it must part; aft, it is preparing the water the propeller must work in. Treating the whole hull as one resistance problem is the standard way to lose marks on this question.

blocks.h: 2. How hull form optimisation is now done, and what changed

blocks.p: The modern method is parametric hull modelling driven by computational fluid dynamics: the hull is described by a set of variables the computer can move - fullness distribution, shoulder position, bulb parameters, buttock slopes - and hundreds or thousands of variants are evaluated numerically against an objective function. Only the shortlist goes to the towing tank, which remains the verification step because it is physical measurement rather than computation. The tank has not been replaced; it has been moved to the end of the process instead of the beginning, which is what allows so much of the design space to be searched.

The important change, however, is not computational, it is conceptual. Forms are now optimised over an operating profile - a realistic distribution of speeds, draughts, trims and loading conditions - rather than at a single contract design point. Slow steaming made the single-point optimum wrong. Ships designed for a service speed found themselves trading permanently well below it, on a hull whose bulb, shoulder and entrance had all been shaped for a condition they no longer used. A profile-optimised form is marginally worse at the contract speed and materially better across the range actually worked, and the second of those is what the ship is paid on. The same logic drives trim optimisation in service, which is the operational shadow of the same idea.

Scope - the bulbous bow's volume, length, section shape and immersion; the entrance angle at the waterline; the stem profile; the position and sharpness of the forward shoulder; and the distribution of fullness forward, which is what actually decides where the hull begins to push water sideways.

Impact - the forebody attacks the wave-making component, and separately the added resistance in waves, which matters a great deal because ships spend their lives in a seaway rather than in calm water and a form optimised only for flat water flatters itself. The bulb works by generating its own wave system, out of phase with the wave made by the stem, so that the two partially cancel. That cancellation is a function of speed and of draught, because the bulb must be at the right immersion for its wave to be the right size. It follows that a bulb tuned for one condition can be actively harmful in another: off-design it adds wetted surface and its own resistance while cancelling nothing. This is where the profile-optimisation point bites hardest, and it is why bulb replacement became a real retrofit market and is one of the very few genuine hull-form measures available to a ship already in service.

A softer entrance and a well-placed shoulder also reduce the tendency to slam and to lose speed voluntarily in head seas, which is an energy saving that never appears in a calm-water model test but is felt on every voyage.
Scope - the run aft, the buttock slopes, the stern and skeg form, bossings and shaft exits, the propeller aperture and the clearances around the disc.

Impact - here the common error is to treat this as another resistance problem. Its principal job is the quality of the water it delivers to the propeller. Because the hull drags a boundary layer with it, the water arriving at the propeller is already moving forward relative to the sea, and it is doing so unevenly - slower directly behind the skeg, faster outboard. That distribution is the wake field, and a blade turning through it meets a different angle of attack at every position in its revolution. A uniform wake field therefore governs cavitation, hull pressure pulses, vibration and blade erosion; a distorted one costs efficiency on every revolution and shortens the life of the blade and the bearings.

So the aftbody improves the propulsive coefficient - the same thrust is obtained from less delivered power - and it does so largely without altering resistance at all. A secondary but real effect is the control of flow separation: too steep a run aft and the flow detaches from the hull, which is precisely the viscous pressure component. Aftbody shaping should be carefully distinguished from bolt-on energy saving devices - ducts, pre-swirl stators, rudder bulbs and fins - which address the same wake problem by adding hardware rather than by changing form. They are relevant to mention, but they are not what the question asked.

Scope - the stern is divided into two longitudinal skegs carrying two shafts and two propellers, in place of a single centreline screw. It is a whole-stern architectural choice rather than a refinement, and it must be taken at the design stage.

It is chosen for a specific and increasingly common case: hulls of high block coefficient operating at restricted draught. On such a ship there is simply not enough water under the counter to swing a propeller of the diameter the power demands, and a propeller that is too small for its power is an inefficient propeller no matter how well it is designed. Rather than accept that, the designer splits the problem in two.

Impact - each propeller sits in cleaner, more nearly axial inflow, because each skeg presents a much smaller wake shadow than a single deep centreline skeg, so each blade works closer to its open-water efficiency. The arrangement permits a larger effective diameter at lower revolutions for the power absorbed, which is the efficient direction of travel for any propeller. Vibration and cavitation fall, because the inflow is more uniform. And the ship gains genuine propulsion redundancy, which has an operational and commercial value quite separate from fuel.

The costs are real and a good answer states them plainly: greater wetted surface and therefore more frictional resistance, which is the direct penalty; two shaft lines with their bearings, seals and alignment; duplicated machinery to buy, install, maintain and certify; a more complex and heavier stern structure; and a higher build cost. The arrangement is therefore a considered trade for a particular hull, not a general improvement, and the trade is only won where the single-propeller alternative is genuinely compromised.

blocks.h: 6. What limits the gains, and where they are measured

ul: The three measures are not additive. They interact through the same flow field, and the combined gain is always less than the sum of the separate claims.
Every figure is ship-specific and conditional on the operating profile actually worked. A gain quoted without its profile is not a gain.

Hull form is one of the few genuine levers on attained EEDI for a new ship and on attained EEXI for an existing one, because most other EEXI routes reduce the ship's capability rather than improve her.

EEXI and the operational carbon intensity indicator have applied since 1 January 2023, so at this sitting the regime was in its first year and the design decision had just acquired a direct regulatory consequence.
In service the benefit appears in the operational indicator, which measures what the ship actually did rather than what she was designed to do.
Hull and propeller fouling can erase the entire gain. A form optimised in the tank and then left unmaintained in service is not an optimised hull.

blocks.p: The examiner has printed three items and two words - scope and impact. That is the structure handed to you: three sections, and within each one a scope paragraph and an impact paragraph. What earns the marks above a pass is the two framing steps at the front, which show you understand why form matters at all, and the closing step, which shows you know the gains are conditional and where they are measured. A candidate who writes only the three middle sections has described three things without answering the question, which asked about improving energy efficiency.

blocks.h: The one distinction most candidates miss

blocks.p: The forebody is a resistance problem. The aftbody is a propeller-inflow problem. They are not two halves of the same task. Forward you are trying not to make waves; aft you are trying to hand the propeller clean, even water. If you write the aftbody section as though it were about resistance you will produce a paragraph that is not wrong but scores very little, because it misses the entire mechanism.

ul: Treating the bulbous bow as an unconditional good. It is tuned to a speed and a draught, and outside that window it can cost more than it saves.
Writing the aftbody section as a second resistance section - see above.
Presenting twin skeg as simply better. It adds wetted surface and a whole second propulsion train; it is a trade made for a specific hull.
Quoting percentage savings. They are ship-specific, baseline-dependent and profile-dependent, and an unsupported number invites the examiner to ask where it came from.
Adding the three gains together. They interact.
Forgetting to say where the benefit is measured - the question is about energy efficiency, which now has instruments attached to it.

Energy saving devices are not hull form. A duct or a pre-swirl stator is hardware bolted on; the question asks about optimising the form. Mention them to show you know the difference, do not answer with them.

The design point trap. The single most valuable sentence in this answer is that slow steaming made single-point optimisation obsolete. It shows you understand why this is a live subject rather than a textbook one.
Fouling. A candidate who describes a beautifully optimised hull and never mentions that a fouled hull loses the lot has answered as a designer rather than as a chief engineer.
Do not import later law. At this sitting the efficiency regime is Annex VI chapter 4 with EEXI and the carbon intensity indicator in their first year. Nothing later belongs in this answer.
Why does a bulbous bow work? - it generates a wave system that partially cancels the bow wave; the cancellation depends on speed and draught, so the benefit is conditional.
What is the wake field and why does it matter? - the distribution of water velocity across the propeller disc; a non-uniform field causes cavitation, pressure pulses, vibration and efficiency loss.
Why would you fit twin skegs? - high block coefficient and restricted draught, where a single propeller cannot be given adequate diameter.
What does twin skeg cost you? - wetted surface, a second shaft line and duplicated machinery.
Which of the three can be done to a ship already in service? - realistically only forebody work, principally bulb replacement, and even that is draught- and speed-conditional.
How would you know in service whether the gain was real? - by the operational carbon intensity indicator, against a clean-hull baseline, with hull and propeller condition accounted for.

blocks.p: FRONT - BACK - SPLIT. Front is about waves. Back is about the propeller's water. Split is what you do when there is no room for a proper propeller. Then SCOPE then IMPACT inside each, and finish on limits and measurement.

ul: MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4, regulations 22 and 24 - attained and required EEDI, the new-ship design index.
MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4, regulations 23 and 25 - attained and required EEXI, the existing-ship index, applying from 1 January 2023.
MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4, regulation 28 - the operational carbon intensity indicator, also applying from 1 January 2023.
Resolution MEPC.328(76) - the revised Annex VI that carries chapter 4 in this form, in force 1 November 2022.
The hydrodynamics itself is naval architecture, not regulation, and is not cited as an instrument.

blocks.p: No percentage gain is asserted anywhere in this answer, for any of the three measures. Published figures exist but they are ship-specific, depend entirely on the baseline and operating profile assumed, and no primary source for any of them is held. Stating a mechanism you can defend is worth more in the examination room than a number you cannot. The MARPOL Annex VI regulations are cited at identity level only and no Annex VI text is quoted, consistent with the standing corpus position that Annex VI is citation-ready rather than quotation-ready. On currency, the most recent MEPC session at this sitting is MEPC 80, of July 2023; nothing from any later session is relied on.

questions.understand_first: Everything a ship burns is spent pushing water out of the way. The hull has to part the water ahead of it, drag a skin of it along its sides, and then close the flow again behind - and each of those costs power. Push a hull faster and one of those costs in particular starts to run away: the ship begins making waves, and the energy in those waves is energy the engine paid for and will never get back. So the shape of the hull is not decoration. It is the single largest decision anybody makes about how much fuel the ship will ever burn, and it is made once, on paper, years before the first litre is bought. There are really two separate shape problems, at opposite ends of the ship. At the front, the job is to part the water without making waves - a matter of how sharply the hull enters, how the fullness is carried back, and whether a bulb is fitted to throw a wave that cancels the one the stem makes. At the back, the job is completely different and it is easy to miss: the aft shape is not really about resistance at all, it is about the quality of the water it hands to the propeller. A propeller working in disturbed, uneven flow loses efficiency, vibrates, and erodes itself. So a good run aft is one that delivers water to the disc smoothly and evenly. And once you accept that, one radical option follows naturally. If a ship is very full-bodied and cannot draw much water - which describes most modern bulk and container ships - there is simply nowhere to fit a propeller big enough to work efficiently. So you stop trying, split the stern into two separate legs and give each one its own smaller, cleanly-fed propeller. That buys you good inflow and useful diameter, and it costs you more surface for the water to rub against and a second set of everything to buy and maintain. The one idea that ties the whole question together is that a hull is only optimised for the way it is actually used. A shape that is superb at the speed the owner ordered can be mediocre at the speed the market later forces on him - which is exactly what happened when the industry slowed down.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the hull form optimisation question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 why form governs the power needed; 2 how optimisation is now done and what changed; 3 (i) forebody; 4 (ii) aftbody; 5 (iii) twin skeg; 6 what limits the gains and where they are measured. Inside each of 3, 4 and 5, write scope then impact.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem prints three items and the two words scope and impact, so it dictates its own middle structure. The marks above a pass are in steps 1, 2 and 6.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between what forebody and aftbody optimisation are trying to achieve?
retrieval_cards.answer: The forebody is a resistance problem - it shapes the entry and the bulb to reduce wave-making and added resistance in waves. The aftbody is a propeller-inflow problem - it shapes the run aft to deliver uniform water to the propeller disc, which governs cavitation, pressure pulses, vibration and the propulsive coefficient. Confusing the two is the commonest error on this question.
retrieval_cards.why: Most candidates write the aftbody as a second resistance paragraph and lose the entire mechanism.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is a bulbous bow's benefit conditional rather than automatic?
retrieval_cards.answer: The bulb generates its own wave system which partially cancels the wave made by the stem. That cancellation depends on the speed and the draught at which the ship is running. Outside the window it was designed for, the bulb can cost more in wetted surface and added resistance than it saves - which is why slow steaming made many existing bulbs wrong and why bulb replacement became a retrofit measure.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the link between the hydrodynamics and the operating-profile point that carries the whole answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the trade a twin skeg arrangement actually makes.
retrieval_cards.answer: It buys cleaner, more axial inflow to each propeller and permits a larger effective diameter at lower revolutions on a full, draught-restricted hull, plus lower vibration and propulsion redundancy. It costs greater wetted surface and therefore frictional resistance, two shaft lines with their bearings and seals, duplicated machinery to maintain, and a higher build cost.
retrieval_cards.why: Presenting twin skeg as simply better, with no cost side, is how candidates show they have memorised rather than understood.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does hull form efficiency get measured, and what was operative at October 2023?
retrieval_cards.answer: In MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4: attained and required EEDI for new ships at regulations 22 and 24, attained and required EEXI for existing ships at regulations 23 and 25, and the operational carbon intensity indicator at regulation 28. EEXI and the carbon intensity indicator have applied since 1 January 2023, so at this sitting the regime was in its first year.
retrieval_cards.why: The question is about energy efficiency, which by this sitting had instruments attached to it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why can the gains from the three named measures not simply be added?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because they act on the same flow field. A better wake aft changes what the propeller demands; a changed forebody alters the flow arriving aft; a twin-skeg stern changes the whole propulsive arrangement. The combined result is always less than the sum of the separately claimed gains, and every figure is specific to the ship and to the operating profile assumed.
retrieval_cards.why: Adding quoted percentages is the fastest way to show the numbers were memorised rather than understood.

blocks.h: 1. Where the survey obligation comes from, and the two regimes running in parallel

blocks.p: Two survey regimes run over every ship at once and they have different sources. Statutory surveys derive from the conventions - SOLAS, the Load Lines Convention and the MARPOL Annexes - and are the responsibility of the flag State. Classification surveys derive from the classification society's own published rules and are contractual, between the society and the owner. In practice a single society usually performs both, acting as a recognized organization under SOLAS regulation XI-1/1 and the RO Code; but the Administration delegates the work, never the responsibility.

The harmonized system of survey and certification placed both regimes on one five-year cycle with a common anniversary date and combinable attendances, which is why an annual survey today is a single event rather than several. The survey types on that cycle are the annual, intermediate, periodical and renewal surveys, together with bottom and tailshaft surveys. It is worth stating precisely that the survey types are created by SOLAS chapter I; the Assembly guidelines - at this sitting resolution A.1156(32) of 2021 - are recommendatory and supply the item lists rather than the obligation.

blocks.h: 2. A) The purpose of annual surveys

blocks.p: The certificates are valid for five years. The purpose of the annual survey is to ensure that the confidence those certificates express is renewed every year rather than assumed for five. Specifically:

ul: To confirm that the ship, her machinery and her equipment are still in the condition in which they were certified, and that she has not been altered without approval.

To give practical effect to SOLAS chapter I regulation 11, which requires that the condition of the ship and her equipment be maintained to conform with the regulations after survey. The annual survey is the mechanism by which that continuing obligation is tested.
To detect deterioration, neglect, unapproved modification, and missing, expired or untested equipment - the failures that arise from how a ship is operated rather than from how she was built.
To provide the endorsement on the certificate, without which the certificate ceases to be valid whatever its printed expiry date.
To keep the flag State, and through it port State control, satisfied that the ship remains compliant between renewals.

blocks.p: It is important to characterise it correctly: an annual survey is a general inspection to confirm maintenance, not a re-examination. The surveyor does not re-open the machinery or re-prove the design; he satisfies himself that what was proved once is still being looked after. It is carried out within three months either side of each anniversary date, and that window is what makes it plannable around the ship's trading.

blocks.h: 3. B) Items examined - hull, closing appliances and load line

blocks.p: The list below is representative and not exhaustive; the actual scope follows the certificates the ship carries and her type. It is best written by walking the ship in a fixed order.

ul: Shell plating and weather decks so far as accessible - corrosion, wastage, cracking, indents, and the condition of previous repairs.
Hatch covers and coamings - structural condition, cleats and securing, compression bars, gaskets and drainage arrangements.
Watertight and weathertight closing appliances - doors, side scuttles and deadlights, ventilators, air pipes and their automatic closures.
Freeing ports and their flaps; guard rails, bulwarks, gangways, walkways and the means of safe access to the ship.
Load line marks and draught marks - legible, correctly positioned and unobscured, with the conditions of assignment still satisfied.
Hatchway beams, ventilator coamings, and the securing arrangements for deck fittings.
Anchoring and mooring arrangements so far as they fall within the certificates.

blocks.h: 4. B) Items examined - machinery, electrical, fire and life-saving

ul: General condition of the main and auxiliary machinery and their seatings, and in particular evidence of oil leakage onto hot surfaces and of oil-soaked lagging.
Steering gear including the auxiliary and emergency arrangements, the communication with the bridge, and the posted operating instructions.
Emergency source of electrical power, its starting arrangements and its changeover, tested on load; emergency lighting and the emergency switchboard.
Bilge pumping and drainage arrangements, bilge level alarms, quick-closing valves, remote stops and machinery space ventilation closures.
Fire main, fire pumps and the emergency fire pump, hydrants, hoses and nozzles; fixed fire-extinguishing systems and their periodic surveys; portable extinguishers.
Fire detection and alarm systems, fire dampers, the fire control plan, and the marking and clearance of the means of escape.

Life-saving appliances - survival craft and rescue boat, davits and launching appliances, liferafts and evidence of their servicing, lifebuoys, lifejackets, immersion suits, EEBDs, line-throwing appliance, pyrotechnics in date, the muster list and the embarkation arrangements.
Radio installations and their power supplies as covered by the relevant certificate; navigation lights, shapes and sound signals; and the charts and nautical publications.

blocks.h: 5. B) Items examined - pollution prevention, and the documentary set

ul: Oil filtering equipment with its 15 ppm alarm and automatic stopping device; that no bypass is fitted; and the sludge, bilge holding and discharge arrangements including the standard discharge connection.
The Oil Record Book, and whether it reconciles with the plant actually fitted; and the IOPP certificate supplement, and whether it still describes the installation.
Sewage treatment or holding arrangements and the discharge connection; the garbage management plan and record book; the incinerator where fitted.
MARPOL Annex VI items - bunker delivery notes and their retained representative samples, engine documentation, and the ship's energy efficiency documentation.
Certificates - validity, correct endorsement, and agreement between what they describe and what is on board.
Continuous Synopsis Record; the minimum safe manning document; the ISM Document of Compliance and Safety Management Certificate; the ISPS ship security certificate; and the MLC documentation.
The class survey status itself - which surveys are due, and what conditions of class are outstanding and when they fall due - together with the record of previous port State control inspections.

blocks.h: 6. C) Condition of class - what it is and how one arises

blocks.p: A condition of class is a requirement imposed by the classification society that a specific measure be carried out by a specific date, in order that the ship's class be retained. Some societies use the term recommendation, or record the item in a memorandum; the vocabulary varies between societies but the concept does not. It should be stated precisely that this is a classification-society term and not a convention term - it is created by the society's rules and the class contract, not by SOLAS.

One arises when a survey, or a report of damage or defect, discloses something that is genuinely wrong but which does not make the ship unfit to proceed. The society is not confined to passing or failing the ship. It records the defect, fixes a scope and a due date, and the ship retains her class in the meantime. A condition of class is therefore best understood as permission to continue on terms, occupying the ground between full compliance and suspension. It is closed only when a surveyor attends and confirms the required measure has been carried out - and, crucially, it is recorded in the ship's class status, where other people can read it.

ul: It identifies a real defect and fixes a date. The rectification does not become optional because the ship was allowed to sail.
It may impose operational restrictions in the interim - a tank or space not to be used, a loading or draught restriction, or a limitation on the use of a system.
It drives repair and docking planning, spares procurement, and the timing of the next class attendance, and so it consumes management attention as well as money.
It should be entered in the planned maintenance system and in the ship's defect and risk registers, so that it is tracked rather than remembered.
If it is allowed to fall overdue, class is liable to be suspended or withdrawn. That is the point at which a manageable item stops being manageable.

Because SOLAS regulation II-1/3-1 requires a ship to be designed, constructed and maintained in compliance with the rules of a recognized organization, loss of class is not merely a private contractual matter - it becomes a SOLAS non-compliance.

And where the society also acts as the recognized organization issuing statutory certificates, those certificates are liable to fall with the class. That is the chain by which a deferred technical item becomes a detention.

blocks.h: 8. C) The commercial consequences, and why they are the larger ones

blocks.p: The technical consequence of a condition of class is bounded by the defect: fix the item by the date and it closes. The commercial consequence is not bounded at all, and the reason is that the class status is visible to third parties.

ul: Charterers. Time charter forms conventionally warrant that the vessel is in class and will be maintained in class throughout the period. An overdue condition of class can put the owner in breach of that warranty, with consequences for hire and for off-hire claims.

Vetting and terminal acceptance. Inspectors and terminal operators read outstanding items as evidence of how the ship is managed. An open item, and still more a pattern of them, can cost a fixture outright - and it does so without any regulator being involved.

Insurance. Hull and machinery cover is conventionally conditioned on class being maintained, so a suspension can prejudice cover at exactly the moment it is needed; the P&I position is similar. The underwriter's interest is not in the defect but in what the record says about the management.
Port State control. An outstanding condition of class is a targeting factor, and it can supply the clear grounds for a more detailed inspection that the ship would otherwise have avoided.
Sale and finance. It affects the price obtainable, the buyer's due diligence, and loan covenants which commonly require class to be maintained without outstanding conditions.

blocks.p: The management conclusion follows directly from the asymmetry. Conditions of class are closed early, never at the due date, because the due date leaves no margin for a missed port or an unavailable surveyor. And a condition of class that recurs - the same item, survey after survey - should be treated not as a repair to be repeated but as a failure of the maintenance system, and investigated as one.

The examiner has printed the marks - 4, 6 and 6 - and they tell you exactly how to spend the time. Limb A is worth four marks and is a purpose question: five or six crisp reasons, not a page. Limb B is worth six and is explicitly a list, so it must be written as a list and it must be ordered, because an unordered list looks like whatever the candidate happened to remember. Limb C is worth six and is the only limb with any analysis in it, because it asks for a comparison of commercial against technical impact - and the answer to that comparison is that they are not symmetrical.

blocks.h: The idea that makes the annual survey explicable

blocks.p: The certificate lasts five years; the confidence cannot. An annual survey is a general inspection to confirm that the ship is still being maintained - it re-proves nothing and re-opens nothing. Its real subject is the owner's upkeep. That single sentence generates the purpose limb and it also explains the scope: the surveyor looks hardest at the things that fail through neglect rather than through wear.

blocks.h: How to write the list limb without freezing

blocks.p: Do not try to recall a list. Walk the ship in a fixed order and the items come to you: OUTSIDE (hull, decks, hatches, closing appliances, load line), then INSIDE (machinery, steering, emergency power, bilges, fire, life-saving), then PAPERS (pollution equipment and records, certificates, class status). Three headings, six or seven items under each, and you have written a properly ordered six-mark answer in five minutes. Always add the sentence that the list is representative and not exhaustive - it is true, and it protects you from an examiner asking why you omitted something.

ul: Describing the annual survey as though it were a renewal survey. It is a general inspection; it does not re-examine what was proved at construction.
Writing limb B as unstructured prose. The examiner asked for a list; give him a list, and order it.
Defining condition of class as a deficiency. It is not. It is a requirement to do a specific thing by a specific date, and the ship keeps her class in the meantime.

Treating condition of class as a statutory concept. It is a class concept; the statutory consequence arrives indirectly, through SOLAS II-1/3-1 and through the certificates the society issued as a recognized organization.
Answering limb C's comparison by listing the same consequences twice. The point is the asymmetry: the technical consequence is bounded by the defect, the commercial one is not.
Forgetting the three-month window either side of the anniversary date - a cheap, precise mark.

Condition of class is not a detention and it is not a non-conformity. Three different regimes, three different issuers, three different consequences. Keeping them apart is the mark of a management-level answer.
The Administration delegates the work, not the responsibility. If you describe the classification society as the authority, you have got the architecture wrong.
The survey types come from SOLAS chapter I, not from the Assembly guidelines. The guidelines are recommendatory and give the item lists.
Do not cite the 2023 Assembly survey guidelines at this sitting. The 33rd Assembly did not adopt until 6 December 2023, two months after this paper. The applicable resolution is A.1156(32) of 2021.

An overdue condition of class is the trap that closes the whole answer: class suspended, SOLAS II-1/3-1 breached, statutory certificates prejudiced, ship detained. Say the chain out loud - it is the difference between a description and an analysis.
When is the annual survey due? - within three months either side of each anniversary date of the certificate.

What is the difference between an annual and an intermediate survey? - the intermediate is a deepening of the annual at the second or third anniversary, taking the place of one annual survey on the construction certificate.
Who imposes a condition of class? - the classification society, under its own rules and the class contract. Not the flag State and not the port State.

What happens if it goes overdue? - class is liable to be suspended or withdrawn; through SOLAS II-1/3-1 that becomes a SOLAS non-compliance, and statutory certificates issued by that society as an RO are prejudiced.
How would a charterer find out? - the class status is visible; and most time charters warrant that the ship is and will be maintained in class.

What would you do as Chief Engineer on receiving one? - record it in the PMS and the defect register with its scope and due date, plan the rectification and the surveyor's attendance well inside the date, and report it to the Company. If the same item recurs, investigate the maintenance system rather than repeating the repair.

blocks.p: WHY - WHAT - WHAT IF NOT. Why the survey exists (limb A), what is looked at (limb B, walked OUTSIDE - INSIDE - PAPERS), and what happens when something is found but the ship still sails (limb C, which splits into THE SHIP and THE MARKET).

ul: SOLAS chapter I, regulations 6 to 10 - the survey and inspection regime, including the annual survey of structure, machinery and equipment.
SOLAS chapter I, regulation 11 - maintenance of conditions after survey. The provision that gives the annual survey its purpose, and the single most useful citation on this question.
SOLAS chapter I, regulation 19 - control; how a port State enforces what the survey certified.
SOLAS regulation II-1/3-1 - design, construction and maintenance to recognized class rules. The hinge by which loss of class becomes a SOLAS non-compliance.
SOLAS regulation XI-1/1 and the RO Code - the basis on which a society does statutory work for an Administration.
The 1988 SOLAS and Load Lines Protocols - which introduced the harmonized system; the Load Lines Convention 1966 annual survey; and the MARPOL Annex surveys brought onto the same cycle.
Resolution A.1156(32), Survey Guidelines under the HSSC, 2021 - the applicable Assembly guidelines at this sitting. Recommendatory.
Condition of class - classification-society practice. Not an instrument, and not cited as one.

blocks.p: Three limits are recorded and each is stated in the answer itself. First, the list of items examined is expressly representative and not exhaustive: no single instrument prints a closed list, and the real scope follows the certificates carried, the ship type and the surveyor's judgement on the day. Second, condition of class is a classification-society term, not a convention term, and different societies name it differently - condition of class, recommendation, memorandum item. No society's rule text is held or quoted, so the concept is stated and the variation is named rather than one vocabulary being asserted as universal. Third, the commercial consequences - the charterparty warranty of class, vetting outcomes, the hull and P&I response, and the effect on sale and finance - are reasoned from the mechanism by which class status becomes visible to third parties. No charterparty form, vetting protocol or policy wording was read this session and none is quoted. On currency, the applicable Assembly survey guidelines at this October 2023 sitting are A.1156(32); the 2023 guidelines were not adopted until 6 December 2023 and are not used.

questions.understand_first: A ship's certificates are valid for five years, and the obvious question is what stops her deteriorating for four and a half of them. The answer is that the long certificate is deliberately punctuated: at intervals somebody independent comes aboard and checks that the ship is still the ship she was certified to be. That is all an annual survey is. It is not a re-examination - nobody re-opens the engine or re-measures the plating - it is a general inspection to confirm that what was proved once is still being maintained, and its real subject is the owner's upkeep rather than the ship's design. Once you see it that way the scope explains itself: the surveyor looks at the things that go wrong through neglect rather than through wear - the closing appliances that get left open, the emergency equipment that is never tested, the pollution equipment that gets quietly bypassed, the paperwork that stops matching the ship. The second idea in the question is subtler and is the one candidates fumble. When a surveyor finds something wrong, he has two honest choices and they are not pass and fail. Some defects genuinely make the ship unfit and she stops. But most do not: they are real, they need fixing, and they can safely wait for a repair port or a docking. For those, the society records a requirement to do a specific thing by a specific date, and the ship keeps her class in the meantime. That is a condition of class. It is a permission to continue on terms, and it is written down where other people can see it. And that last point - that it is visible - is where the sting is. The technical consequence of a condition of class is bounded: fix the defect by the date and it goes away. The commercial consequence is not bounded at all, because charterers, vetting inspectors, underwriters, buyers and banks all read the same record, and to them an open item is evidence about how the ship is run.
questions.memory_cue: WHY (2) - WHAT (3, 4, 5) - WHAT IF NOT (6, 7, 8). The examiner's three limbs are purpose, list, condition of class. For the list, walk the ship in a fixed order and never invent one on the day: OUTSIDE - INSIDE - PAPERS, that is hull and closings (3), then machinery, fire and life-saving (4), then pollution and documents (5). For condition of class, WHAT IT IS (6), THE SHIP (7), THE MARKET (8).

steps.title: Where the survey obligation comes from, and the two regimes running in parallel
points: Statutory surveys come from the conventions - SOLAS, Load Lines, MARPOL - and are the flag State's responsibility
Class surveys come from the society's own rules and are contractual, between society and owner
In practice one society usually does both, acting as a recognized organization under SOLAS XI-1/1 and the RO Code
The Administration delegates the work, never the responsibility
The harmonized system put both onto one five-year cycle with a common anniversary date
The survey types on that cycle are annual, intermediate, periodical, renewal, plus docking and tailshaft surveys
At this sitting the applicable Assembly guidelines are A.1156(32) of 2021 - the survey TYPES, however, are created by SOLAS chapter I, not by the guidelines

steps.title: A) The purpose of annual surveys
points: To confirm that the ship is still in the condition in which she was certified - the certificate is five years, the confidence must be renewed yearly
It gives effect to SOLAS chapter I regulation 11: conditions are to be MAINTAINED after survey, and no change made without approval
It is a general inspection, not a re-examination - the surveyor confirms maintenance rather than re-proving design
To detect deterioration, neglect, unapproved modification and missing or expired equipment
To provide the endorsement on the certificate without which it ceases to be valid, whatever its printed expiry
To keep the flag State and, through it, port State control informed that the ship remains compliant
Held within three months either side of each anniversary date, which is what makes it plannable

steps.title: B) Items examined - hull, closing appliances and load line
points: Shell plating and weather decks so far as accessible; visible corrosion, wastage, cracking, indents and previous repairs
Hatch covers and coamings - condition, cleats, compression bars, gaskets, drainage
Watertight and weathertight closing appliances - doors, side scuttles, ventilators, air pipes and their closures
Freeing ports, guard rails, gangways, walkways and means of safe access
Load line marks and draught marks - legible, correctly positioned, not obscured
Bulwarks, hatchway beams, ventilator coamings and their securing
Anchoring and mooring arrangements so far as they are covered by the certificates

steps.title: B) Items examined - machinery, electrical, fire and life-saving
points: General condition of main and auxiliary machinery, seatings, and evidence of oil leakage onto hot surfaces
Steering gear, including the auxiliary and emergency arrangements, communications and the posted instructions
Emergency source of electrical power and its changeover, tested on load; emergency lighting
Bilge pumping and drainage, bilge alarms, quick-closing valves and remote stops
Fire main, pumps and hydrants, hoses and nozzles; fixed and portable extinguishing systems and their surveys
Fire detection and alarm, dampers, ventilation stops, fire control plan and the means of escape
Life-saving appliances - boats, davits and launching gear, liferafts and their servicing, lifebuoys, lifejackets, immersion suits, EEBDs, muster list and embarkation arrangements
Radio and navigational equipment as covered by the relevant certificate; lights, shapes, sound signals, charts and publications

steps.title: B) Items examined - pollution prevention, and the documentary set
points: Oil filtering equipment and the 15 ppm alarm and automatic stopping device; no bypass fitted; sludge and bilge arrangements
Oil Record Book reconciling with the plant, and the IOPP certificate supplement matching what is actually installed
Sewage plant and the discharge arrangement; the garbage management plan and record book; incinerator
Annex VI items - bunker delivery notes and retained samples, engine documentation, and the ship's energy efficiency documentation
Certificates - validity, endorsements, and that the ship matches what they describe
Continuous Synopsis Record, safe manning document, ISM DOC and SMC, ISPS certificate, MLC documentation
The class survey status itself - outstanding conditions of class and their due dates, and the record of previous port State inspections
The list is representative and not exhaustive - the scope follows the certificates the ship carries and her type

steps.title: C) Condition of class - what it is and how one arises
points: A requirement imposed by the classification society that a specific measure be carried out by a specific date in order that class be retained
Some societies call it a recommendation; the concept is the same and the vocabulary varies
It is a classification term, not a convention term - say so, it is the precision the examiner is looking for
It arises when a survey finds a defect that does not make the ship unfit to proceed but must still be corrected
It is therefore permission to continue on terms, and it sits between full compliance and suspension
It carries an owner, a scope and a due date, and is closed only by a surveyor's attendance and confirmation
It is recorded in the ship's class status, which is the fact that generates everything in step 8

steps.title: C) The technical consequences
points: It identifies a real defect and fixes a date by which it must be rectified - the defect does not become optional
It may impose operational restrictions in the meantime - a tank or space not to be used, a loading restriction, a limitation on a system
It drives repair and docking planning, spares procurement and the timing of the next class attendance
It feeds into the planned maintenance system and into the ship's own defect and risk registers
If it falls overdue, class is liable to be suspended or withdrawn
And because SOLAS II-1/3-1 requires the ship to be maintained in compliance with recognized class rules, loss of class becomes a SOLAS non-compliance
Statutory certificates issued by that society as a recognized organization are then liable to fall with the class - which is how a technical item becomes a detention

steps.title: C) The commercial consequences, and why they are the larger ones
points: The class status is visible to third parties, and that visibility is the whole commercial mechanism
Charterers - most forms warrant that the vessel is and will be maintained in class; an overdue item can put the owner in breach
Vetting and terminal acceptance - open items are read as evidence of how the ship is run, and can cost a fixture outright
Insurance - hull cover is conventionally conditioned on class being maintained, so suspension can prejudice cover; P&I likewise
Port State control - an outstanding condition of class is a targeting factor and can supply clear grounds
Sale and finance - it affects price, due diligence and loan covenants that require class to be maintained
The asymmetry is the point. The technical consequence is bounded by the defect; the commercial consequence propagates to everyone who reads the record
Hence the management response: close conditions of class early, never at the due date, and treat a recurring one as a system failure rather than a repair

quick_revision.recall_15s: Framework. Two regimes - statutory (conventions, flag State) and class (society's rules, contractual). Usually one society does both, as a recognized organization under SOLAS XI-1/1 and the RO Code; the Administration delegates the work, not the responsibility. Harmonized system = one five-year cycle, common anniversary date, combinable attendance. Types: annual, intermediate, periodical, renewal, plus bottom and tailshaft. Types come from SOLAS chapter I; the Assembly guidelines at this sitting are A.1156(32) and are recommendatory. A) Purpose. Confirm the ship is still as certified; give effect to SOLAS I/11, maintenance of conditions after survey; detect deterioration, neglect, unapproved modification and missing or untested equipment; provide the endorsement without which the certificate is invalid; keep flag and port State satisfied. It is a general inspection, NOT a re-examination. Held within three months either side of each anniversary date. B) Items - walk the ship: OUTSIDE, INSIDE, PAPERS. OUTSIDE - shell and decks, hatch covers and coamings, closing appliances, air pipes and ventilators, freeing ports, guard rails, load line and draught marks. INSIDE - machinery general condition and oil leaks on hot surfaces, steering incl. emergency, emergency power tested ON LOAD, bilge pumping and alarms, quick-closing valves and remote stops, fire main and pumps, fixed and portable systems, detection and dampers, means of escape, LSA - boats, davits, rafts serviced, lifejackets, immersion suits, EEBDs, muster list. PAPERS - 15 ppm equipment and stopping device, no bypass, ORB reconciling, IOPP supplement matching, sewage, garbage plan, Annex VI BDNs and retained samples, certificates and endorsements, CSR, safe manning, DOC and SMC, ISSC, MLC, and the class survey status with outstanding conditions of class. List is representative, NOT exhaustive. C) Condition of class. A requirement to carry out a specific measure by a specific date in order that class be retained. Some societies say recommendation. A CLASS term, not a convention term. Arises where a defect is real but does not make the ship unfit - permission to continue on terms. Closed only by a surveyor's attendance. Technical impact - real defect with a date; possible operational restriction; drives docking and spares planning; goes in the PMS; if overdue, class suspended or withdrawn; SOLAS II-1/3-1 then makes that a SOLAS non-compliance and RO-issued statutory certificates fall with it - detention. Commercial impact - it is VISIBLE: charterparty warranty of class breached; vetting and terminal refusal; hull and P&I cover conditioned on class; PSC targeting and clear grounds; sale price and loan covenants. The asymmetry is the answer - technical is bounded by the defect, commercial is not. So close conditions early, never at the due date, and treat a recurring one as a system failure.
critical_numbers: Annual survey: within three months either side of each anniversary date
Certificate cycle: five years, on a common anniversary date under the harmonized system
SOLAS chapter I regulation 11 - maintenance of conditions after survey
SOLAS regulation II-1/3-1 - designed, constructed AND MAINTAINED to recognized class rules
SOLAS regulation XI-1/1 and the RO Code - recognized organizations
Resolution A.1156(32) - Survey Guidelines under the HSSC, 2021. The applicable guidelines at this sitting
A.1186(33) is FUTURE - adopted 6 December 2023, two months after this sitting
quick_revision.critical_regulation: SOLAS chapter I regulation 11 - maintenance of conditions after survey - is the regulation behind limb A: after any survey, the condition of the ship and her equipment shall be maintained to conform with the regulations, and no change shall be made without approval. That continuing obligation is what the annual survey exists to test. SOLAS regulation II-1/3-1 is the regulation behind limb C: because a ship must be designed, constructed and maintained in compliance with the rules of a recognized organization, a suspension of class becomes a SOLAS non-compliance rather than a private contractual matter. The Assembly survey guidelines applicable at this sitting are A.1156(32) of 2021, and they are recommendatory - the survey types themselves are created by SOLAS chapter I.
quick_revision.major_trap: Defining a condition of class as a deficiency, or as a statutory item. It is neither: it is a classification-society requirement that a specific measure be carried out by a specific date in order that class be retained, and the ship keeps her class in the meantime. The second trap is answering limb C by listing the same consequences under two headings - the examiner asked for commercial versus technical, and the answer is the asymmetry: the technical consequence is bounded by the defect, the commercial one propagates to every charterer, vetting inspector, underwriter, buyer and bank who reads the class record. The third is citing the 2023 Assembly survey guidelines: they were adopted on 6 December 2023, two months after this sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the annual survey and condition of class question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 the two survey regimes and the harmonized cycle; 2 A) the purpose of annual surveys; 3 B) items - hull, closings and load line; 4 B) items - machinery, electrical, fire and life-saving; 5 B) items - pollution and documents; 6 C) what a condition of class is; 7 C) technical consequences; 8 C) commercial consequences.
retrieval_cards.why: The printed marks are 4, 6 and 6, so the list limb gets three steps and condition of class gets three.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the purpose of an annual survey, in one sentence?
retrieval_cards.answer: To confirm that the ship, her machinery and her equipment are still in the condition in which they were certified and are being maintained, giving effect to SOLAS chapter I regulation 11. It is a general inspection to confirm maintenance, not a re-examination, and it provides the endorsement without which the five-year certificate ceases to be valid.
retrieval_cards.why: The 'general inspection, not re-examination' characterisation is what separates a correct answer from a description of a renewal survey.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define a condition of class.
retrieval_cards.answer: A requirement imposed by a classification society that a specific measure be carried out by a specific date in order that class be retained. Some societies call it a recommendation. It arises where a defect is real but does not make the ship unfit to proceed, so it is permission to continue on terms. It is a classification term, not a convention term, and is closed only by a surveyor's attendance.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates routinely define it as a deficiency, which loses the whole mechanism.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Trace what happens if a condition of class is allowed to go overdue.
retrieval_cards.answer: Class is liable to be suspended or withdrawn. Because SOLAS II-1/3-1 requires a ship to be designed, constructed and maintained in compliance with recognized class rules, loss of class becomes a SOLAS non-compliance. Statutory certificates issued by that society as a recognized organization are prejudiced with it, and the ship becomes detainable at the next port State inspection.
retrieval_cards.why: This chain is how a deferred technical item becomes a detention, and it is the analytical high point of the answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is the commercial impact of a condition of class larger than the technical impact?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the technical consequence is bounded by the defect - fix it by the date and it closes - while the commercial consequence is unbounded, since the class status is visible to third parties. Charterers hold a warranty of class, vetting inspectors and terminals read open items as evidence of management quality, hull and P&I cover is conditioned on class, port State control uses it for targeting, and buyers and lenders rely on it.
retrieval_cards.why: The question asks for commercial versus technical, so the asymmetry is the answer rather than two lists.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do you write the six-mark list limb without freezing?
retrieval_cards.answer: Walk the ship in a fixed order rather than recalling a list. OUTSIDE - shell and decks, hatch covers, closing appliances, air pipes and ventilators, freeing ports, load line and draught marks. INSIDE - machinery and oil leaks, steering including emergency, emergency power tested on load, bilge and quick-closing valves, fire systems, life-saving appliances. PAPERS - 15 ppm equipment and Oil Record Book, garbage and sewage, certificates, and the class survey status.
retrieval_cards.why: An ordered list reads as knowledge; an unordered one reads as whatever the candidate remembered.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Assembly survey guidelines apply at an October 2023 sitting, and which do not?
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution A.1156(32), Survey Guidelines under the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification, 2021, adopted by the 32nd Assembly in December 2021. A.1186(33) does NOT apply: the 33rd Assembly did not adopt until 6 December 2023, two months after this sitting. In either case the guidelines are recommendatory - the survey types are created by SOLAS chapter I.
retrieval_cards.why: The 33rd Assembly boundary is the sharpest temporal trap on this paper and it reaches this question as well as Q3.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When is an annual survey due, and what is the window?
retrieval_cards.answer: At each anniversary date of the certificate, within a window of three months either side of that anniversary. The anniversary date is common across the harmonized certificates, which is what allows the annual, intermediate and periodical surveys to be taken in a single attendance.
retrieval_cards.why: A cheap, precise mark that candidates lose by giving a vague answer.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three limbs of increasing difficulty, and the marks say so. Limb A is a four-mark definition of PURPOSE and is testing whether the candidate knows the difference between what a survey is for and what a survey does. Limb B is a six-mark recall limb, explicitly a LIST, and is testing breadth and order. Limb C is a six-mark analytical limb and is the real question: it asks not only what a condition of class is but how its commercial and technical impacts differ, which at management level is asking whether the candidate understands that class status is a commercial instrument as well as a technical one.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: Printed and internally consistent: A (4), B (6), C (6), summing to sixteen. The route follows that split exactly - one framing step, one step for limb A, three steps for the six-mark list limb so it can be written in a defensible order, and three steps for the six-mark condition-of-class limb split into definition, technical and commercial. The framing step is not asked for and is kept short.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: For A, the annual survey correctly characterised as a general inspection confirming maintenance rather than a re-examination, with SOLAS I/11 identified and the three-month window given. For B, an ORDERED and reasonably comprehensive list covering hull and closing appliances, machinery and emergency systems, fire and life-saving, pollution prevention equipment and records, and the documentary set including the class survey status - with the list acknowledged as non-exhaustive. For C, a correct definition that does not confuse a condition of class with a deficiency, the technical consequences including the overdue chain through SOLAS II-1/3-1, and a genuine comparison showing that the commercial consequences are the larger because class status is visible to third parties.
primary_source_plan: SOLAS chapter I regulations 6 to 11 and 19, and SOLAS II-1/3-1 and XI-1/1, at corpus IDENTITY level - the statutory survey architecture and the hinge between class and SOLAS
The harmonized cycle, common anniversary date and three-month window carried from the MIW verification record for QP2304-Q9, where they were established
The Assembly survey guidelines RE-DERIVED for this sitting: A.1156(32) of 2021, NOT A.1186(33) which is two months future
The examination list built from the scope of the certificates endorsed at an annual survey, and stated as representative rather than exhaustive
Condition of class from settled classification practice, carried as authoritative secondary and expressly identified as a class term rather than a convention term
The commercial consequences reasoned from the visibility mechanism; no charterparty form, vetting protocol or policy wording read or quoted
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - The statutory architecture is long settled and the survey practice moves slowly. The live risk is the ASSEMBLY GUIDELINES CITATION, where both available family donors cite a 33rd Assembly resolution that is two months future at this sitting, and the temptation to carry it is real.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW to MEDIUM. The survey regime is convention-based and of general application. Where an Indian-flag ship is concerned the surveys are administered under the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 and the rules made under it; the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 did not commence until 15 March 2026 and is excluded. No Indian statutory provision is cited by number.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: No instrument prints a closed list of items examined at an annual survey, so no complete list can be asserted and the answer says so. The vocabulary for a condition of class varies between societies - condition of class, recommendation, memorandum item - and no single society's term is asserted as universal. The boundary between a condition of class and an outstanding statutory deficiency is real but is often blurred in practice; the answer keeps them separate and names the difference in issuer and consequence.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Eight numbered sections. A short prose framing step; a prose-plus-bullet purpose section; three bulleted list sections walking the ship outside, inside and through the papers; a prose definition of condition of class; a bulleted technical-consequence section ending on the overdue chain; and a bulleted commercial section closing on the asymmetry and the management response.

reuse_evidence: TIER B - FAMILY COVERAGE OF THE SUBJECT, NOT OF THE TASK, adjudicated by reading every port State control stem in the corpus. There are six of them and NONE asks this paper's three limbs. QP2312-Q2 and QP2606-Q2 ask the legal framework and the right of appeal against detention; QP2406-Q3 asks clear grounds, detainable deficiencies and PR17; QP2504-Q2 asks clear grounds, disagreement with a detention and the review panel. WHAT IS REUSED, AND IT IS THE FRAMING STEP ONLY: the account of what port State control is and the enabling control provisions in each convention, from QP2312-Q2 step 2 (December 2023). That material is settled and is the correct place to take the legal basis from.

WHAT IS NOT REUSED AND IS ENTIRELY FRESH: the regional agreements limb, the future limb and the effectiveness limb. In particular the EVALUATIVE limb - is port State control an effective tool - has no analogue anywhere in the corpus, and the balanced case for and against it was reasoned rather than carried.

questions.question_delta: NOT THE SAME QUESTION AND NOT A CLOSE ONE. QP2312-Q2 asks (a) the concept of port State control with focus on the legal framework and (b) the rights of appeal where a ship has been detained unreasonably. THIS PAPER ASKS NEITHER LIMB. It asks (i) regional cooperation and agreements, (ii) the future of port State control, and (iii) whether port State control is an effective tool for ship safety. WHAT WAS DONE: the legal-framework material is DEMOTED to a single short framing step, because this paper wants it as context rather than as content; the entire appeal, detention and clear-grounds apparatus is DROPPED; and three substantial limbs were authored fresh. THE ASSEMBLY REVERSAL IS THE CRITICAL DELTA AND IT AFFECTS EVERY AVAILABLE DONOR. The 33rd IMO Assembly adopted resolution A.1185(33), Procedures for Port State Control, 2023, on 6 DECEMBER 2023 - TWO MONTHS AFTER THIS SITTING. blocks.h: 1. What port State control is, and the power it rests on

blocks.p: Port State control is the inspection of foreign ships in national ports to verify that the ship, her equipment and her crew comply with the requirements of the international conventions, and that she is manned and operated in accordance with them. It is a safety net beneath the flag State: it supplements the flag State's primary responsibility and does not transfer it.

The power is not general. It is conferred convention by convention, each carrying its own control article: SOLAS regulation I/19, with regulations IX/6, XI-1/4 and XI-2/9 for the ISM, operational-requirement and security regimes; MARPOL articles 5 and 6; Load Lines article 21; STCW article X and regulation I/4; Tonnage article 12; AFS article 11; BWM article 9; and MLC 2006 Title 5.2. Above them UNCLOS supplies the framework - article 94 on flag State duties, articles 218 and 219 on port State enforcement, and article 226 on the limits of inspecting foreign vessels.

IMO's own consolidated Procedures for Port State Control are recommendatory: the Assembly invites Governments to implement them. At this sitting the applicable resolution is A.1155(32), adopted by the 32nd Assembly in December 2021. Finally, the principle that makes the whole system workable is no more favourable treatment: a ship whose flag State is not a Party, or which falls below a convention's size threshold, is given no advantage by that fact. Without it, the cheapest response to any new convention would be not to ratify it.

blocks.h: 2. (i) Why the cooperation had to become regional

blocks.p: A single State inspecting on its own achieves surprisingly little. It sees a snapshot of one call and knows nothing of how the ship looked at her previous four ports. Its inspectors may spend the morning re-checking a vessel that another authority cleared last week, while a genuinely substandard ship sails past unexamined. And where national standards diverge, the substandard operator simply engages in port shopping and calls where enforcement is lightest.

Ships also trade in regional patterns, so a region is the natural unit over which a ship can actually be followed from call to call. The chosen instrument is deliberately not a treaty. A memorandum of understanding is an administrative arrangement between maritime authorities rather than an agreement between States; it requires no ratification, can be concluded quickly, and can be amended as fast as practice moves. That flexibility is precisely why the regional model spread.

ul: Paris MoU - Europe and the North Atlantic. The oldest of the regimes, established in the early 1980s in the aftermath of a major tanker casualty, and the model on which the others were built.
Tokyo MoU - Asia and the Pacific, and the largest by volume of traffic covered.

Indian Ocean MoU - India is a member. Inspections in Indian ports are carried out by surveyors of the Directorate General of Shipping under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and the rules made under it.
Vina del Mar Agreement - Latin America; the Caribbean MoU; and the Mediterranean MoU.
Abuja MoU - West and Central Africa; the Black Sea MoU; and the Riyadh MoU covering the Gulf States.
The United States Coast Guard is a deliberate exception: it operates its own national port State control programme rather than joining a memorandum, and applies its own targeting matrix.

blocks.p: IMO's role across all of this is coordination, harmonisation and technical cooperation - it publishes the Procedures and supports the regimes, but it does not run any of them and has no inspectors of its own. No membership figure, inspection volume or detention rate is stated here, because those numbers are administrative and change every year.
The value of a regional agreement lies almost entirely in what the members share. In practice that means:

ul: A common regional database of inspections, deficiencies and detentions, accessible to every member authority. This is the core of the arrangement; everything else is built on it.
Harmonised procedures, checklists and deficiency codes, so that a finding recorded by one authority means the same thing to another.

A ship risk profile - built from the performance of her flag, the performance of her recognized organization, her type, her age and her own inspection history - which determines how frequently and how thoroughly she is inspected.
Avoidance of duplicated inspection: a ship inspected recently within the region is not normally re-inspected within the period, which releases scarce inspector time onto the ships that warrant it.
Concentrated inspection campaigns, in which every member examines one chosen topic during the same window. These produce genuinely comparable data and exert a real, visible deterrent for a season.
Published performance lists for flag States and for recognized organizations, which apply reputational and commercial pressure where the regime has no legal power at all.
Detention review arrangements, so that an owner who believes a detention unjustified has somewhere to take it - which disciplines the regime as well as protecting the owner.
Training, harmonisation seminars and exchanges of officers between authorities, because consistency between inspectors is the regime's most persistent weakness.

blocks.h: 5. (ii) The future of port State control

ul: Data-driven targeting. The direction of travel is toward richer risk profiling and better use of reported data, so that inspection effort follows evidence of risk rather than a rotation.

Digitalisation. Electronic certificates and the means to verify them, single-window reporting, and remote access to the ship's documentation - shifting inspector time away from paper checking and toward the condition of the ship.

Remote and hybrid inspection. This developed rapidly out of necessity when physical access was restricted, and it remained under active discussion. It is useful for documents and for pre-screening; it is no substitute for walking the machinery space, and the regimes have been careful about that.

A widening scope. Port State control now reaches far beyond hull and machinery: labour conditions under MLC 2006, ballast water management, anti-fouling systems with the cybutryne controls applying from 1 January 2023, and now energy efficiency, since the EEXI and carbon intensity regime under MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 has applied since 1 January 2023 and brings its documentation within the inspector's reach.
Cyber security. Maritime cyber risk management must be addressed in the safety management system, which means it is reachable on an ISM-related inspection rather than requiring any new control power.
Alternative fuels. LNG is in service and methanol and ammonia are in prospect. This creates a real competence gap: the constraint on inspecting these ships is inspector training, not legal authority.
The human element. An increasing share of findings concerns hours of rest, fatigue, crew familiarity and seafarer welfare rather than hardware - which is where the causes of accidents actually live.
Quality over quantity, and the professionalisation of the port State control officer: fewer, better-targeted and above all more consistent inspections.
Greater harmonisation between regimes, and in the long term the ambition of genuinely global data exchange in place of separate regional pools.

blocks.h: 6. (iii) The case that it is effective

ul: It reaches ships that the flag State does not and sometimes will not. No other mechanism in the system does this, and that alone justifies it.
The deterrent effect is larger than the inspection effect. Far more ships are maintained to a standard because they expect to be inspected than are ever actually caught by an inspection.
No more favourable treatment removed the commercial reward for non-ratification. That is a structural achievement, not merely an operational one.
Performance lists for flags and recognized organizations create commercial and reputational consequences that no regulation could impose directly.
Detention is a commercially serious sanction - lost time, lost charter, damaged reputation and heavier future targeting - so it genuinely alters owner behaviour.
It generates the only large independent evidence base on the real condition of the world fleet, and that evidence feeds back into rule-making.
Concentrated inspection campaigns can be shown to move fleet behaviour on a chosen topic within a single season.
Taken together, substandard operation is now materially harder and more expensive to sustain than it was before the regime existed.
An inspection is a snapshot in port. It is not a survey and it is certainly not a voyage; it sees the ship at the moment she is most prepared.
It is reactive. It finds deficiencies that already exist; it does not prevent them arising.
Consistency is the persistent weakness - between individual inspectors and between regimes. That is a fairness problem for owners as well as a safety problem.
Ships are, and always will be, prepared for inspection. A clean engine room on the day proves less than it appears to.
Deficiencies are symptoms. The causes lie ashore in manning levels, maintenance budgets and commercial pressure, and only the ISM route reaches them at all - and then only indirectly.
Coverage is uneven. Regimes differ greatly in resources, and a ship trading only where enforcement is weakest is inspected least, which is exactly the wrong way round.
It has no direct power over a flag State. It can publish a performance list; it cannot compel an Administration to do anything.
Detention statistics are a poor measure of success. Falling detentions may mean a better fleet - or fewer inspections, or softer ones.

There is a real institutional risk of port State control being relied on as a substitute for flag State implementation and company safety management. It can never be that, and treating it as such would be a systemic failure.

blocks.h: 8. (iii) The verdict, and what it depends on

blocks.p: Yes, it is an effective tool - but it must be judged as what it is, a safety net and a deterrent, rather than as a primary means of producing safety. Measured against that purpose it has been demonstrably effective at the bottom of the market, which is precisely where it was aimed; and it is least effective at the top, where a well-run ship gains little from an inspection she was always going to pass.

Its effectiveness is also conditional, and the conditions are worth naming: on the competence of the inspector, on consistency between inspectors and regimes, on honest and complete data, and on regional coverage reaching the trades where enforcement is weakest. Where those conditions fail, the tool fails with them.

The correct conclusion is therefore that port State control is a complement, not a replacement. Safety is built by the flag State's implementation and by the company's safety management system; port State control verifies and deters. And the right measure of it is behaviour changed rather than deficiencies recorded - which is why the deterrent effect matters more than the detention statistic. For the Chief Engineer that translates into something quite practical: a ship kept ready for inspection every day is a genuinely safe ship, and a ship prepared the night before is neither safe nor, in the end, reliably clear of detention.

The stem prints three items and gives them no separate marks, so they should be treated as roughly equal and each must be genuinely answered. The commonest failure on this question is to write everything the candidate knows about port State control - clear grounds, detainable deficiencies, the detention procedure, the right of appeal - none of which is asked. That material belongs to a different question and earns nothing here. The framing step is deliberately short: it establishes the legal basis in one place so that limbs (i), (ii) and (iii) can each be given proper room.

blocks.h: The idea that makes limb (i) explicable

blocks.p: The value of a regional agreement is the sharing, not the inspecting. Any State could inspect ships in its own ports without any memorandum at all. What it cannot do alone is know what the ship looked like at her last four ports, avoid wasting effort on a vessel a neighbour cleared last week, or apply a consistent standard so that the operator cannot simply call somewhere else. A common database, a common procedure and an agreed targeting rule are the entire point. If you write that sentence, the whole limb follows from it.

blocks.h: How to make limb (iii) a real answer rather than an opinion

blocks.p: The examiner has asked a genuine question - is it effective - so it needs a genuine argument, which means a case for, a case against and a verdict that follows from both. The discipline that keeps it honest is to judge the tool against its own purpose: it is a safety net. Judged as a net it is effective, because it catches what would otherwise get through. Judged as a substitute for the flag State it fails, because it was never that. A candidate who says only 'yes it is very effective' has not answered; nor has one who lists only criticisms.

ul: Answering with clear grounds, detainable deficiencies and the detention procedure. None of it is asked.
Listing memoranda with no account of why the cooperation is regional or how it works. The names alone are worth very little.
Quoting membership numbers, inspection totals or detention rates. They change every year and an unsupported figure invites a question you cannot answer.

Treating limb (ii) as speculation. It is not - digitalisation, risk-based targeting, the widening scope into labour, ballast water, anti-fouling and energy efficiency, and the alternative-fuel competence gap are all observable directions with evidence behind them.
Writing limb (iii) as either uncritical praise or pure criticism. The mark is in the balance and in the verdict.
Forgetting no more favourable treatment. It is the single most quotable principle in the whole subject.
Port State control does not transfer the flag State's responsibility. If your answer reads as though the port State has taken over, the architecture is wrong.
A memorandum of understanding is not a treaty. It binds maritime authorities administratively, which is exactly why it is quick to agree and quick to amend. Saying so is a precise, cheap mark.
The IMO Procedures are recommendatory. Governments are invited to implement them; the binding power lives in the conventions' own control articles.

Do not cite the 2023 Procedures at this sitting. Resolution A.1185(33) was adopted on 6 December 2023, two months after this paper. The applicable resolution here is A.1155(32) of December 2021. This is the sharpest temporal trap on the whole paper.
The United States is not in a memorandum. Naming that exception shows you know the map rather than a list.
Detention numbers are not a measure of effectiveness. Saying why is the analytical high point of limb (iii).
Which memorandum does India belong to? - the Indian Ocean MoU; inspections in Indian ports are carried out by the Directorate General of Shipping.
What is no more favourable treatment? - a ship whose flag is not a Party to a convention, or which is below its size threshold, gets no advantage from that; she is held to the same standard.
Why a memorandum rather than a convention? - it is an administrative arrangement between authorities, needs no ratification, and can be amended as quickly as practice changes.
What decides how often a ship is inspected? - her risk profile: flag performance, recognized organization performance, ship type, age and her own inspection history.
What is a concentrated inspection campaign? - all members of a regime examine one chosen topic in the same window, producing comparable data and a visible deterrent.

Is port State control making ships safer? - it is effective as a deterrent and a safety net, most so at the bottom of the market; it cannot replace flag State implementation or the company's safety management system.
Which resolution contains the IMO Procedures? - at this sitting, A.1155(32) of 2021. Recommendatory.
