retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the NOx, SAM and EGR question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 why NOx forms and the three levers; 2 A) primary measures; 3 A) secondary measures; 4 A) the comparison, on six axes; 5 A) the regulatory frame; 6 B) scavenge air moisturizing; 7 B) exhaust gas recirculation; 8 B) the two compared and what they share. Limb A must end in an actual comparison - 'vis-a-vis' is an instruction.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming the three levers first lets every later technology be introduced by which lever it pulls, so the answer reads as one argument.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What decides whether a NOx measure is primary or secondary, and where does EGR fall?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is decided by where the NOx goes, not by where the equipment sits. A primary measure means less NOx is ever created; a secondary measure means NOx already formed is destroyed. Exhaust gas recirculation is therefore PRIMARY, even though its scrubber, cooler and blower are all external plant, because its effect is that the NOx is never formed.
retrieval_cards.why: Classifying by hardware location is the single commonest error on this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the three levers every NOx control measure pulls.
retrieval_cards.answer: Peak flame temperature - add something that absorbs heat or raises the charge's specific heat. Oxygen availability - displace part of the oxygen with inert gas. Residence time at peak - shorten the time at maximum temperature through injection timing and rate shaping. And the governing trade-off is that a hot, fast, oxygen-rich burn is exactly what thermal efficiency wants, so almost every measure costs fuel.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the organising idea of the whole subject and it makes every technology explicable in one sentence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Describe scavenge air moisturizing and name its safety-critical component.
retrieval_cards.answer: Water is evaporated into the scavenge air downstream of the charge air cooler, often in a multi-stage humidification section with re-heat between stages. Latent heat of evaporation plus the higher specific heat of water vapour both lower the peak temperature. The water must be fresh and clean because it reaches the cylinder. The safety-critical component is the water mist catcher: vapour must enter the cylinder, never droplets.
retrieval_cards.why: The mist catcher is what candidates omit, and it is the item on which the whole system's safety turns.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Describe exhaust gas recirculation and explain why it reaches further than humidification.
retrieval_cards.answer: Part of the exhaust is scrubbed, cooled, passed through a mist catcher and returned to the scavenge air by an EGR blower, with shut-off and change-over valves and an adapted turbocharger arrangement. It pulls two levers at once: it reduces the oxygen concentration of the charge and it raises the charge's specific heat through carbon dioxide and water vapour. That is why it can reach the strictest tier on its own, where humidification pulls temperature only.
retrieval_cards.why: Two levers against one is the whole comparison in limb B.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is selective catalytic reduction demanding to fit and to run?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is temperature-sensitive, which decides whether the reactor sits before or after the turbine; sulphur-sensitive, since salts form at low temperature and blind the catalyst; dependent on accurate dosing, or unreacted reagent passes through as ammonia slip; and it introduces a reagent, a tank and a supply chain. It also occupies space and adds exhaust back pressure, both severe constraints in a retrofit.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the only mature secondary measure, so the whole secondary case rests on it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What do scavenge air moisturizing and EGR both do to the cylinder, and how is it managed?
retrieval_cards.answer: Both put water and acid where the engine's designer did not intend them. Water reaching the liner disturbs the oil film, and acid attacks the surfaces. Both therefore transfer a burden onto cylinder lubrication - correct feed rate, correct base number for the duty - and onto its monitoring, of which scrape-down analysis is the principal means.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the closing observation that marks out an operating engineer rather than a reader.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the structure of MARPOL Annex VI regulation 13 without quoting a limit, and which text applies at October 2023.
retrieval_cards.answer: Three tiers, each limit a function of the engine's rated speed; the construction date fixes the tier; the strictest tier additionally depends on where the ship operates, giving two modes whose changeover is recorded with date, time and position; an output threshold applies and certain emergency engines are excluded; certification under the NOx Technical Code 2008 as revised, with in-service compliance through the NOx Technical File. The applicable text is the Revised Annex VI from MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022.
retrieval_cards.why: The structure is worth more marks than a remembered number, and it avoids quoting from a text the corpus does not clear for quotation.

blocks.h: 1. What GISIS is, and the problem it solves

blocks.p: The Global Integrated Shipping Information System (GISIS) is a web-based information platform developed and maintained by the IMO Secretariat. Its existence answers a structural feature of the Organization: IMO has no inspectorate and no ships. Almost everything it knows about how its instruments are working in practice comes from what Member States report to it. Before GISIS that reporting was done by paper circular - slow to compile, scattered across separate documents, and very difficult to search or compare. GISIS consolidates into one system the information that States are required or invited to report under the various instruments.

It should be classified correctly at the outset, because the classification governs the rest of the answer: GISIS is an administrative platform, not an instrument. It creates no obligation of its own. The obligations live in the conventions; GISIS is the channel through which they are discharged and, more importantly, the means by which the resulting information is made useful.

ul: To provide a single point of collection and dissemination for information related to IMO instruments.
To support Member States in implementing and enforcing those instruments, by giving Administrations and port State control access to information held by others.
To give the Organization the evidence base on which instruments are reviewed, amended and developed - so that policy rests on reported experience rather than on assertion.
To promote transparency and information sharing between Administrations, and with industry where the data is public.
To reduce duplicated reporting, each item being collected once and made available to all who need it.

blocks.h: 3. The functions - how it works and what it holds

blocks.p: GISIS is organised into modules, each corresponding to a reporting obligation or a defined information set. Those in use include - and this list is not exhaustive - marine casualties and incidents; piracy and armed robbery against ships; reception facilities, including reports of their inadequacy; contact points for Administrations and national authorities; recognized organizations authorised by flag States; ship and company particulars; port State control information; and modules covering pollution prevention equipment, survey and certification, maritime security and facilitation.

The operating model is straightforward. Data is entered by designated national focal points in each Member State, and the Secretariat administers the system rather than generating the content. Access is tiered: some modules are open to the public, others are restricted to Member States or to registered users, according to the sensitivity of the data. Records are searchable and exportable, and that is the feature which converts a pile of individual reports into usable evidence. In doing so the system facilitates data sharing among Member States, letting one Administration see what another has reported without bilateral correspondence.

blocks.h: 4. The fuel oil module and MARPOL Annex VI

blocks.p: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14 caps the sulphur content of fuel oil used on board - 0.50 % m/m globally since 1 January 2020, and 0.10 % m/m within emission control areas. But the Annex also recognises a practical reality: a ship cannot burn fuel that is not on sale. Regulation 18, on fuel oil availability and quality, therefore requires Parties to take reasonable steps to promote the availability of compliant fuel oil, and provides that where a ship cannot obtain compliant fuel oil despite best efforts, it reports that fact to its Administration and to the competent authority of the port of destination - the mechanism commonly known as the fuel oil non-availability report. Regulation 18 also provides for the ship to notify its Administration and the port State where a supplier has failed to meet the requirements, for example on the bunker delivery note or the representative sample.

The GISIS module collects these reports centrally. It should be distinguished from the separate Annex VI reporting stream under regulation 27, the collection and reporting of ship fuel oil consumption data, which is a different obligation serving a different purpose - efficiency and carbon intensity rather than sulphur compliance. Confusing the two is easy and it is worth a sentence to keep them apart.

ul: It gives a single standard channel and format, replacing ad hoc correspondence with several authorities in several different forms.
The ship's own report becomes a preserved record, which is precisely what supports her position if the fuel actually used is later questioned at a port State inspection.
The report identifies the port and the supplier concerned, so it is actionable rather than merely noted.
Reports of genuine non-availability are kept distinct from reports of supply that failed to meet requirements - two different problems needing two different responses from two different parties.
The Administration and the port State receive the same record, which removes an obvious source of dispute about what was reported and when.

blocks.p: The analytical value is considerably greater than the reporting value, because aggregation changes what the data means. A single non-availability report tells you about one ship on one day. Several hundred, searchable by port and by date, tell you something quite different:

ul: Where compliant fuel is genuinely unavailable - a map of the real supply position, as opposed to the assumed one.
Which ports recur, and which suppliers repeatedly fail on quality or on documentation.
Risk-based targeting for port State control: inspectors can concentrate on ships that have bunkered where problems cluster, rather than inspecting at random.
Evidence for the Organization in reviewing how regulation 18 is working and whether availability is adequate - a review that is itself an obligation, and one that needs data to be meaningful.

Separating genuine non-availability from evasion. This is the point that matters most to an honest operator. If a ship claims non-availability at a port where everyone else bunkered compliant fuel that week, the claim stands out - and, just as importantly, a genuine claim is corroborated by the pattern.
Commercial use - bunker planning, supplier selection and voyage planning, where the data is publicly accessible.

blocks.p: A management-level answer must state the limitations, because they govern how much weight the data will bear:

ul: It is a reporting system. Its completeness depends entirely on States and ships actually reporting, and under-reporting is likely - a ship that quietly bunkers non-compliant fuel does not file a report.
Therefore the absence of reports from a port is not evidence that compliant fuel was available there. It may equally mean that nobody reported.

Module membership and structure are administrative: modules are added, merged and reorganised without any instrument being amended, so any list of modules dates quickly - which is why the list above is given as non-exhaustive.

A GISIS record is evidence that a report was made, not a finding of fact. It does not determine whether the ship's efforts to obtain compliant fuel were genuinely reasonable - that remains for the Administration and the port State to judge.

It supplements and does not replace the ship's own evidence: the bunker delivery note and its retained representative sample, the oil record book, and the correspondence showing the attempts actually made to obtain compliant fuel.

blocks.p: The stem prints no lettered limbs but sets two tasks, and the second one names its own two halves: reporting and analysing. Splitting those into separate sections is the single easiest structural decision on this question, because most candidates blur them into one paragraph about 'usefulness' and in practice only ever answer the reporting half. Closing on the limits of the data is what makes it a management-level answer rather than a description of a website.

blocks.h: The idea that makes GISIS explicable

blocks.p: IMO has no inspectors. It knows only what States tell it. GISIS exists so that what they tell it arrives in one place, in one format, and can be searched. Every aim and every function follows from that one fact - and so does every limitation, because a system built entirely on reporting can never be complete.

blocks.h: Why aggregation is the real answer to 'usefulness'

blocks.p: One non-availability report is an anecdote. Several hundred, searchable by port and date, are evidence - about where compliant fuel actually is, which suppliers keep failing, and which non-availability claims look genuine against the pattern. If you make that point explicitly you have answered 'analysing' properly; if you do not, you have written the reporting half twice and lost half the second task.

ul: Describing GISIS as if it imposed obligations. It is a platform; the obligations are in MARPOL Annex VI.
Answering 'usefulness' only in terms of reporting, and never addressing analysis.
Presenting a module list as complete and current. It is administrative and changes without any amendment - say so.
Confusing the regulation 18 availability and quality stream with the regulation 27 fuel oil consumption data reporting stream.
Omitting the limitations. At management level, knowing what data cannot prove is part of the answer.
Drifting into port reception facilities. A closely related question at another sitting asks for that; this one does not.
Absence of reports is not evidence of availability. The most attractive wrong inference available from this data set, and the best single sentence in the answer.
The stem's own premise - 'recently GISIS updated its module on fuel oil' - should be accepted and used, not argued with. Anchor the answer to the sitting.
This paper asks about the fuel oil module only. Do not answer the wider question that another sitting asked.
A GISIS record proves a report, not a fact. Whether the ship's efforts were reasonable is still for the authorities.
Regulation 18 and regulation 27 are different streams. One is about being able to buy compliant fuel; the other is about how much fuel you burned.
Do not import later law. The most recent MEPC session at this sitting is MEPC 80 of July 2023; nothing from MEPC 81 or later belongs here.

What would you retain aboard to support a non-availability report? - the correspondence with suppliers and agents showing the attempts made, the bunker delivery notes, the retained representative sample, the oil record book and the voyage plan.
Who enters the data into GISIS? - designated national focal points in each Member State; the IMO Secretariat administers the system.
What is the sulphur limit and since when? - 0.50 % m/m globally since 1 January 2020, and 0.10 % m/m in emission control areas.
How does a port State inspector use this? - to target inspections at ships that bunkered where problems cluster, and to test a non-availability claim against the pattern for that port.
Is GISIS public? - partly. Access is tiered, with some modules public and others restricted to Member States.
Which regulation requires the non-availability report? - Annex VI regulation 18, fuel oil availability and quality. Regulation 27 is the separate consumption-data stream.
Does filing the report make the ship compliant? - no. It evidences that a report was made; whether the efforts were reasonable is for the Administration and the port State.

blocks.p: WHAT - AIM - FUNCTION for the first task; MODULE - REPORT - ANALYSE - LIMITS for the second. The examiner has given you two of the seven step names in the stem itself: reporting and analysing.

ul: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14 - sulphur content of fuel oil; 0.50 % m/m globally from 1 January 2020, 0.10 % m/m in emission control areas.
MARPOL Annex VI regulation 18 - fuel oil availability and quality; the non-availability report, and notification where a supplier has failed to meet requirements. The regulation behind this question.
MARPOL Annex VI regulation 27 - collection and reporting of ship fuel oil consumption data. A separate stream, named in order to be distinguished.
MARPOL Annex VI regulation 17 - reception facilities, named only as one of the GISIS modules.
Resolution MEPC.328(76) - the Revised MARPOL Annex VI, in force 1 November 2022 and therefore the applicable text at this sitting.
GISIS itself is an administrative platform of the IMO Secretariat, not an instrument, and is not cited as one.

blocks.p: Three limitations are recorded. First, the module list is expressly non-exhaustive: modules are added and reorganised administratively, without any instrument being amended, so no fixed complete set is asserted for this or any date. Second, the MARPOL Annex VI regulations are cited at identity level only and no Annex VI text is quoted, consistent with the standing corpus position that Annex VI is citation-ready rather than quotation-ready. Third, the stem's premise that the module had 'recently' been updated is accepted as the examiner's own framing and anchored to the sitting; no release date was verified. On currency, the applicable Annex VI text at this sitting is that introduced by MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022, and the most recent MEPC session is MEPC 80, of 3 to 7 July 2023 - the session that adopted the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy on 7 July 2023, which October is unambiguously after. MEPC 81 of March 2024 and everything later are future and nothing from them is relied on.

questions.understand_first: A convention only works if the governments that signed it can see what is actually happening under it. The Organization that made the rules has no inspectors and owns no ships; almost everything it knows comes from what governments choose to send it. For decades that meant paper circulars - a State would report a casualty or a problem, the Secretariat would summarise it, and by the time anybody could use the information it was old, scattered across several documents and effectively unsearchable. The system in this question is the answer to that: one place where the information States are required or invited to report is collected, stored and made searchable, so that the same fact can serve a policy debate, a port inspector and a shipowner planning a voyage. It is worth being precise about what it therefore is - an administrative platform, not an instrument. It creates no obligation of its own; the obligations live in the conventions, and this is simply the channel through which they are discharged and the information made useful. The fuel oil part of the question illustrates why any of this matters. The rules cap how much sulphur a ship may burn, but they also recognise a practical reality: a ship cannot burn fuel that is not for sale. So if compliant fuel genuinely cannot be obtained despite real effort, the ship reports that fact rather than being punished for it. One such report on its own is not very interesting - it tells you about one ship on one day. Collected in one searchable system, several hundred of them become something quite different: evidence about which ports actually have compliant fuel and which suppliers keep failing. And that is exactly what a regulator, an inspector and a chartering department each need, for three entirely different reasons.

blocks.h: 1. a) What the Convention is, and the bargain it strikes

blocks.p: The LLMC is the Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims, 1976. It was adopted on 19 November 1976 and entered into force on 1 December 1986, replacing the earlier 1957 Convention. Its 1996 Protocol, in force 13 May 2004, substantially raised the limits and introduced a tacit acceptance procedure so that they could be raised again without a diplomatic conference; amendments adopted under that procedure in 2012 took effect on 8 June 2015. In India the Convention is given effect through Part XA of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.

What it does is simple to state: it allows the persons it names to cap their total liability arising out of a single occurrence, by reference to the tonnage of the ship. The bargain it strikes is worth stating explicitly, because the rest of the answer follows from it. The right is near-automatic - Article 2 claims are limitable whatever the legal basis on which liability arose, in contract, in tort or otherwise - and in exchange it is near-unbreakable.

blocks.h: 2. a) Its purpose - why the law permits a cap at all

blocks.p: It is worth confronting the oddity directly: in most fields of law a party at fault pays the whole loss. The reasons maritime law departs from that are practical rather than sentimental.

ul: Insurability. This is the real answer. A liability with a calculable ceiling can be underwritten; a liability with no ceiling cannot be priced and therefore cannot be insured. Without limitation there would be no functioning liability market, and therefore no reliable fund for claimants either.
Certainty and finality. Both sides know the worst case before the casualty rather than after a trial, which is what allows a business to be planned and a claim to be settled.

Encouraging the venture. A ship is a very large concentration of value, sent far from those who own her, doing something inherently hazardous, under the control of people the owner cannot supervise directly.
A fund that actually exists. A claimant with a share of a constituted fund is very often better off than a claimant holding an unsatisfied judgment against a single-ship company with no assets.

Orderly distribution. Once a fund is constituted the Convention bars other actions against the same defendant in respect of the same occurrence, so claimants share rateably instead of racing each other between jurisdictions.

blocks.p: The quid pro quo is that a right so hard to break must be, and is, correspondingly hard to abuse - which is what Article 4 is for.

blocks.h: 3. a) The two heads of claims for which limitation is stated

blocks.p: The general limits are set out in Article 6, and it states the limits under two heads:

ul: Head one - claims in respect of LOSS OF LIFE OR PERSONAL INJURY.
Head two - ANY OTHER CLAIMS, which in practice means claims for damage to property and the consequential losses flowing from it.

blocks.p: Each head has its own separate fund, and each fund is calculated by reference to the ship's tonnage. The life and personal injury fund is the larger of the two, which reflects a deliberate policy choice about what the system values. The two funds are not sealed off from one another in one direction: if the life and personal injury fund is exhausted, the unsatisfied balance of those claims does not simply disappear - it ranks rateably alongside the property claims against the other fund.

One distinction must be made explicitly, because it is where most candidates lose the limb. Claims by passengers are dealt with separately, under Article 7, and are NOT one of the two heads. Article 7 provides its own limit for passenger claims, calculated by reference to the number of passengers the ship is authorised to carry. If you offer passengers as one of the two heads, you have answered a different question.

blocks.h: 4. a) Who can limit liability, and what the Convention never covered

blocks.p: Article 1 confers the right on shipowners and salvors, and both expressions are wider than they look.

ul: 'Shipowner' is defined to mean the owner, charterer, manager and operator of a seagoing ship - so a time charterer or a technical manager may limit in his own right.
A salvor is any person rendering services in direct connexion with salvage operations, including operations to raise, remove or destroy a wreck.
Any person for whose act, neglect or default the shipowner or salvor is responsible - which brings the master, officers and crew within the protection.

The insurer of liability for claims subject to limitation is entitled to the benefits of the Convention to the same extent as the assured. This provision is what makes the cap commercially real, because it is the insurer who ultimately answers.

blocks.p: And the cap was never universal. Article 3 excepts certain claims from limitation altogether: claims for salvage or contribution in general average; claims for oil pollution damage within the meaning of the CLC, which has its own regime; claims subject to any international convention or national legislation governing nuclear damage; and certain claims by servants of the shipowner or salvor whose duties are connected with the ship, where the governing law of the contract of service does not permit limitation. Naming these is what shows the examiner that you understand the cap as a bounded right rather than a blanket immunity.

Plaintiff. The party who brings a civil action - the person asserting the claim, called the claimant in many jurisdictions and in much modern procedure. He bears the burden of proof: he must establish his loss, the breach of duty or of contract, and the causal connection between them. In this context the plaintiff is the party claiming against the shipowner, and it is he who must attack the cap if he wishes to escape it.

Defendant. The party against whom the action is brought and who answers it. In a maritime claim the defendant is typically the shipowner, charterer, manager, operator, salvor, or the liability insurer, and it is the defendant who invokes the limit and constitutes the fund.

Two refinements are worth adding because they show the terms are understood rather than merely recited. First, in a limitation action the procedural roles can invert: the shipowner may himself commence proceedings to establish his right to limit and to constitute the fund, so that the party who would ordinarily be defendant is procedurally the moving party. Second, and more importantly, the burden of breaking the limit lies on the claimant - which, as the next section explains, is precisely why the limit so rarely breaks.

blocks.h: 6. b) Privity - and why it is the OLD test

blocks.p: Privity in this context means knowledge and concurrence: the owner knew of the fault or the state of affairs that caused the loss, and assented to or acquiesced in it. It is knowledge plus acquiescence rather than mere knowledge, and it is personal to the owner himself - or, where the owner is a company, to the individual who is its directing mind - rather than to the crew or to shore staff generally.

Its importance is historical, and stating that is what earns the mark. Under the 1957 Convention and the earlier law, an owner lost the right to limit where the loss occurred with his 'actual fault or privity'. Critically, that test placed the burden on the owner to prove the absence of fault or privity - a negative, and a difficult one. The result was that limitation was broken with some regularity.

Article 4 of the LLMC 1976 replaced that test. A person is no longer entitled to limit if it is proved that the loss resulted from his personal act or omission, committed with the intent to cause such loss, or recklessly and with knowledge that such loss would probably result. Two things changed at once: the standard rose from fault to intent or subjectively-informed recklessness, and the burden moved from the owner to the claimant. That single reversal is why the modern right to limit is described as virtually unbreakable, and it is the reason limitation is now a near-automatic feature of maritime liability rather than a contested one.

Finally, distinguish privity of contract - the separate common-law doctrine that only a party to a contract may sue upon it. It is the same word applied to an unrelated subject, and confusing the two is an easy mark to lose.

blocks.h: 7. b) Unlimited liability - and the three routes to it

blocks.p: Unlimited liability means liability that is not capped by any fund: the defendant answers for the whole of the loss as proved, bounded in practice only by his assets and his insurance. There are three routes to it, and setting them out as three is what turns a definition into an answer.

ul: Route one - the Article 4 conduct is proved. The claimant establishes that the loss resulted from the defendant's own personal act or omission, committed with intent or recklessly with knowledge that such loss would probably result. The right to limit is then lost.

Route two - the claim is an Article 3 excepted claim. Salvage, general average contribution, CLC oil pollution damage, nuclear damage and certain employee claims were never inside the Convention at all, so there is no cap to lose.
Route three - the Convention simply does not apply. The forum State is not a party to it, or the defendant is not among the persons entitled to limit, or he fails to constitute the fund.

blocks.p: The consequence that matters at management level is commercial rather than legal. Once liability is unlimited, the exposure becomes effectively uninsurable - there is no ceiling against which an underwriter can price. That is why the loss of the right to limit is not simply an expensive outcome but the event that the entire liability insurance structure of the industry exists to avoid, and why the conduct described in Article 4 is treated as seriously as it is.

The printed marks are 8 and 8, which is an instruction: limb b) is worth exactly as much as limb a) and must not be written as a four-line glossary tacked on at the end. That is the commonest structural failure on this question - candidates spend twenty minutes on the Convention and four lines on the terms, and lose half the marks available. Give limb b) three proper sections. Limb a) itself contains three separate questions - what and why, the two heads, and who may limit - so it needs three sections of its own, and each of those three questions must be visibly answered.

blocks.h: The idea that makes limitation explicable

blocks.p: Insurability. In most law the party at fault pays the whole loss; maritime law caps it. The reason is not sympathy for shipowners - it is that a liability with no ceiling cannot be priced, and therefore cannot be insured. Without a cap there is no liability market, and without a liability market a claimant's judgment is worth whatever a single-ship company happens to own. The cap exists as much for the claimant as for the owner, and saying so is what turns a recital into an argument.

The two heads under Article 6 are loss of life or personal injury and any other claims. Passengers are NOT one of them - they have a separate limit under Article 7. Every year candidates offer 'personal injury, property, and passengers' as three heads, or 'passengers and cargo' as the two, and lose the limb outright. Learn it as PEOPLE and EVERYTHING ELSE, with passengers in a separate article.

ul: Giving passenger claims as one of the two heads. They are Article 7 and are separate.
Treating the two funds as sealed. If the life fund is exhausted, the balance ranks rateably against the property fund.
Answering 'who can limit' with 'the shipowner'. The definition covers owner, charterer, manager and operator, plus salvors, plus those for whom they are responsible, plus the liability insurer.
Forgetting Article 3. A cap that never applied to salvage, general average, CLC oil pollution or nuclear damage is a bounded right, not a blanket immunity.
Defining privity as mere knowledge. It is knowledge and concurrence, and it is personal to the owner.
Presenting privity as the current test. It is the old test, displaced by Article 4 - and explaining that displacement is where the marks are.
Writing limb b) as a glossary. It carries eight of the sixteen marks.

The burden reversal is the whole point of the privity section. Under the old test the OWNER had to disprove fault; under Article 4 the CLAIMANT must prove intent or informed recklessness. That is why the right is now near-unbreakable.
Article 2 claims are limitable whatever the basis of liability - contract, tort or otherwise. The right does not depend on how the liability arose.
The insurer gets the benefit to the same extent as the assured. That provision is what makes the cap commercially real, and few candidates mention it.
Unlimited liability has three routes, not one. Article 4 conduct is the famous one; Article 3 exception and simple non-application of the Convention are the other two.

Do not import later law. At this sitting the Indian vehicle is Part XA of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. The Merchant Shipping Act 2025 did not commence until 15 March 2026, roughly two and a half years after this paper.
Do not quote a monetary limit. The figures depend on which Protocol and which amendment the State concerned has adopted, and an unsupported number invites exactly the follow-up you cannot answer.
What are the two heads of claim? - loss of life or personal injury, and any other claims. Passengers are a separate limit under Article 7.
What happens if the life fund is exhausted? - the unsatisfied balance ranks rateably with the property claims against the other fund.
Who may limit? - shipowners, meaning owner, charterer, manager and operator; salvors; those for whose acts they are responsible; and the liability insurer to the same extent as the assured.
What claims can never be limited? - salvage and general average contribution, CLC oil pollution damage, nuclear damage, and certain claims by the owner's or salvor's own servants.
What breaks the limit? - proof that the loss resulted from the person's own act or omission, committed with intent to cause it, or recklessly and with knowledge that such loss would probably result.
Who bears that burden? - the claimant. Under the old 'actual fault or privity' test the owner bore the burden of disproving fault, which is why the limit used to break far more often.
What is privity? - knowledge and concurrence in the fault, personal to the owner. It belongs to the old test, not to Article 4.
How does India give effect to the Convention? - through Part XA of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
Why does the industry care so much about keeping the right to limit? - because without a ceiling the exposure cannot be priced and therefore cannot be insured.

blocks.p: Limb a): WHAT - WHY - HEADS - WHO. Limb b): PARTIES - PRIVITY - UNLIMITED. Inside the heads, PEOPLE and EVERYTHING ELSE, with passengers in their own article. Inside privity, OLD TEST, OWNER'S BURDEN, against NEW TEST, CLAIMANT'S BURDEN. Inside unlimited, THREE ROUTES.

ul: LLMC 1976, Article 1 - persons entitled to limit: shipowners, meaning owner, charterer, manager and operator; salvors; those for whom they are responsible; and the liability insurer.
LLMC 1976, Article 2 - claims subject to limitation, whatever the basis of liability.
LLMC 1976, Article 3 - claims excepted: salvage and general average, CLC oil pollution, nuclear damage, certain employee claims.
LLMC 1976, Article 4 - conduct barring limitation. The provision that replaced 'actual fault or privity'. The single most important citation on this question.
LLMC 1976, Article 6 - the general limits, and the two heads of claim. Article 7 - the separate passenger limit.
LLMC 1976, Articles 8, 11, 12 and 13 - unit of account, constitution and distribution of the fund, and the bar to other actions.
1996 Protocol, in force 13 May 2004; 2012 amendments effective 8 June 2015.
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (India), Part XA - the implementing vehicle in force at this sitting.

blocks.p: Four limits are recorded. First, no monetary limit, tonnage band or Special Drawing Right figure is asserted anywhere in this answer. The applicable figures depend on whether the State concerned is party to the bare 1976 Convention, to the 1996 Protocol, or to the Protocol as amended in 2012, and the Convention text was not read this session. The structure of the limits is stated; the numbers are not. Second, the Indian implementing vehicle is identified as Part XA of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 without asserting a ratification instrument, accession date or statutory sub-section that was not read. Third, the four terms in limb b) are terms of general legal usage rather than Convention definitions, and the answer says so; only privity has a specific anchor in maritime limitation law, in the pre-1976 test, and that anchor is identified. Fourth, the statement that the burden under Article 4 rests on the claimant reflects the settled construction of the Convention and is the reason the right is described as near-unbreakable; no judicial authority was read this session and none is cited. On currency, nothing in the LLMC regime moved between the January 2023 sitting at which this question was last answered and this one: the 1996 Protocol has been in force since 13 May 2004 and the raised limits since 8 June 2015.

questions.understand_first: Start with the oddity, because it is what the question is really about. In almost every other field of law, if you cause a loss you pay for it - all of it. Shipping is one of the very few places where the law openly allows a party who is at fault to say: I accept I am liable, and I will pay only up to this figure, and no further. That looks like a licence to be careless until you see why it exists. A ship is a very large amount of value sent a very long way from the people who own her, doing something inherently hazardous, under the control of people the owner cannot supervise and did not meet. If a single bad night could bankrupt the owner, two things follow: nobody sensible invests in ships, and - more practically - nobody can insure them, because an insurer cannot price a risk that has no ceiling. So the law strikes a bargain. The owner gets a ceiling he can calculate in advance from the size of the ship, and in exchange that ceiling is very hard to break and applies almost automatically, whatever the basis on which he was found liable. Everybody knows in advance roughly what the worst case is, the insurance market can therefore exist, and claimants get a fund that is actually there rather than a judgment against an empty company. The second thing to understand is that the cap is not one pot. Claims are sorted into two families - those about people who were hurt or killed, and everything else, which in practice means damaged property. The people claims get the larger pot, because a legal system that valued a bent crane above a dead crewman would not survive contact with public opinion. And if the people pot runs out, those claimants are not simply turned away - they queue alongside the property claimants for what is left. Everything else in the question - who is allowed to use the cap, what breaks it, and what the four legal words mean - hangs off those two ideas.
questions.memory_cue: WHAT (1) - WHY (2) - HEADS (3) - WHO (4) for limb a); then PARTIES (5) - PRIVITY (6) - UNLIMITED (7) for limb b). The printed marks are 8 and 8, so limb b) is a third of the paper's question and must NOT be written as a four-line glossary at the end.

steps.title: a) What the Convention is, and the bargain it strikes
points: The Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims, 1976 - the LLMC
Adopted 19 November 1976; in force 1 December 1986. It replaced the 1957 Convention
The 1996 Protocol, in force 13 May 2004, raised the limits and introduced tacit acceptance
Amendments adopted under that Protocol in 2012 took effect on 8 June 2015
India gives effect to it through Part XA of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958
It caps total liability arising from one occurrence, by reference to the ship's tonnage
The bargain: near-unbreakable, but near-automatic. Article 2 claims are limitable whatever the basis of liability

steps.title: a) Its purpose - why the law permits a cap at all
points: Insurability. A liability with a calculable ceiling can be underwritten; one without a ceiling cannot
Certainty and finality - both sides know the worst case before the casualty, not after the trial
To encourage investment in a venture that is inherently hazardous and conducted far from the owner's supervision
To give claimants a fund that actually exists, rather than a judgment against a company with no assets
To provide a single forum and an orderly distribution instead of a race between claimants in several jurisdictions
The quid pro quo: because the right is so hard to break, it must be, and is, very hard to abuse

steps.title: a) The two heads of claims for which limitation is stated
points: They are set out in Article 6
HEAD ONE - claims for LOSS OF LIFE OR PERSONAL INJURY
HEAD TWO - ANY OTHER CLAIMS, in practice property damage and consequential loss
Each head has its own separate fund, each calculated on the ship's tonnage
The life and personal injury fund is the larger of the two
If the life fund is exhausted, the unsatisfied balance of those claims ranks rateably with the property claims against the other fund
PASSENGER claims are separate again, under Article 7, and are NOT one of the two heads - the commonest error on this limb

steps.title: a) Who can limit liability, and what the Convention never covered
points: Article 1 - shipowners and salvors
'Shipowner' is defined widely: the owner, charterer, manager and operator of a seagoing ship
A salvor is any person rendering services in direct connexion with salvage operations
Any person for whose act, neglect or default the shipowner or salvor is responsible - so the master and crew are covered
The liability insurer, to the same extent as the assured - which is what makes the cap commercially real

Article 3 excepts certain claims from limitation altogether: salvage and general average contribution; oil pollution damage within CLC; nuclear damage; and certain claims by the owner's or salvor's own servants
So the cap is not universal - some liabilities were never inside it

steps.title: b) Plaintiff and Defendant
points: Plaintiff - the party who brings the civil action and asserts the claim; also called the claimant in many jurisdictions
He bears the burden of proving his case - the loss, the breach and the causal link
Defendant - the party against whom the action is brought and who answers it
Here the defendant is typically the shipowner, charterer, manager, operator, salvor or liability insurer
In a limitation action the procedural roles can invert: the shipowner may commence proceedings to establish his right to limit and to constitute the fund
The burden of BREAKING the limit lies on the claimant - which is exactly why the limit so rarely breaks

steps.title: b) Privity - and why it is the OLD test
points: Privity means knowledge and concurrence - the owner knew of the state of affairs or the fault, and assented to it
It is knowledge plus acquiescence, not mere knowledge, and it is personal to the owner or his alter ego
Under the 1957 Convention and earlier law the owner lost the right to limit where the loss occurred with his 'actual fault or privity'
Critically, that test placed the burden on the OWNER to prove the ABSENCE of fault or privity

Article 4 of the LLMC 1976 replaced it. The limit is now broken only where the loss resulted from the person's personal act or omission, committed with intent to cause such loss, or recklessly and with knowledge that such loss would probably result
The burden moved to the claimant and the standard rose. That single change is why the modern right is described as near-unbreakable
Distinguish privity of CONTRACT - the separate doctrine that only a party to a contract may sue upon it. Same word, different subject

steps.title: b) Unlimited liability - and the three routes to it
points: Unlimited liability means liability not capped by any fund - the defendant answers for the loss in full, as proved
Route one - the Article 4 conduct is proved. Intent, or recklessness with knowledge that such loss would probably result
Route two - the claim is an Article 3 excepted claim, and was therefore never inside the Convention at all
Route three - the Convention does not apply: the forum State is not a party, or the owner fails to constitute or is not entitled to the fund
The practical consequence is what matters at management level: the exposure becomes effectively uninsurable
So the loss of the right to limit is not merely expensive - it is the event the whole insurance structure of the industry is built to avoid

quick_revision.recall_15s: What. Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims, 1976 - the LLMC. Adopted 19 Nov 1976, in force 1 Dec 1986, replacing the 1957 Convention. 1996 Protocol in force 13 May 2004 - raised limits, added tacit acceptance. 2012 amendments effective 8 June 2015. India: Part XA of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. It caps total liability from ONE OCCURRENCE by TONNAGE. The bargain: near-automatic, near-unbreakable - Article 2 claims limitable whatever the basis of liability. Why. INSURABILITY - no ceiling means no price means no cover. Plus certainty and finality; encouraging a hazardous venture conducted far from supervision; a fund that actually exists rather than a judgment against an empty company; and orderly rateable distribution instead of a race between jurisdictions. TWO HEADS - Article 6. (1) LOSS OF LIFE OR PERSONAL INJURY. (2) ANY OTHER CLAIMS - in practice property and consequential loss. Separate fund for each, each on tonnage; the life fund is the larger; if the life fund is exhausted the balance ranks RATEABLY against the property fund. PASSENGERS ARE NOT ONE OF THE TWO HEADS - they are Article 7, a separate limit on authorised passenger numbers. WHO - Article 1. Shipowners and salvors. 'Shipowner' = owner, charterer, manager AND operator of a seagoing ship. Salvor = anyone rendering services in direct connexion with salvage. Plus any person for whose act, neglect or default they are responsible - so master and crew. Plus the LIABILITY INSURER, to the same extent as the assured. Article 3 EXCEPTS: salvage and general average contribution, CLC oil pollution, nuclear damage, certain claims by their own servants. b) PLAINTIFF - brings the action, asserts the claim, bears the burden of proof; claimant in modern usage. DEFENDANT - sued, answers, invokes the limit and constitutes the fund; typically owner, charterer, manager, operator, salvor or insurer. In a limitation action the roles can invert - the owner may move first. The burden of BREAKING the limit is on the CLAIMANT. b) PRIVITY = KNOWLEDGE AND CONCURRENCE, personal to the owner or his directing mind - knowledge PLUS acquiescence. It is THE OLD TEST: under the 1957 Convention the limit broke on the owner's 'actual fault or privity', and THE OWNER had to prove its ABSENCE. Article 4 replaced it: broken only by the person's own act or omission, with INTENT to cause such loss, or RECKLESSLY AND WITH KNOWLEDGE that such loss would probably result. Standard rose AND burden moved to the claimant - hence near-unbreakable. Distinguish privity of CONTRACT - only a party may sue on a contract. b) UNLIMITED LIABILITY = not capped; pay the loss in full. THREE ROUTES: (1) Article 4 conduct proved; (2) Article 3 excepted claim - never inside; (3) Convention does not apply - forum State not a party, person not entitled, or fund not constituted. Consequence: effectively UNINSURABLE - which is the event the whole liability structure exists to avoid.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: LLMC 1976 Article 4 - conduct barring limitation - is the single most important provision on this question: a person is not entitled to limit if it is proved that the loss resulted from his personal act or omission, committed with the intent to cause such loss, or recklessly and with knowledge that such loss would probably result. It replaced the pre-1976 'actual fault or privity' test, raising the standard and moving the burden from the owner to the claimant - which is why the modern right is near-unbreakable. Article 6 carries the two heads of claim; Article 7 the separate passenger limit; Article 1 the persons entitled; Article 3 the excepted claims. The 1996 Protocol has been in force since 13 May 2004 and the limits it carries were raised with effect from 8 June 2015. India gives effect through Part XA of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
quick_revision.major_trap: Offering passenger claims as one of the two heads. The two heads under Article 6 are loss of life or personal injury and any other claims; passengers have their own separate limit under Article 7 and are not one of the two. The second trap is presenting privity as the current test - it is the old one, displaced by Article 4, and explaining that displacement, including the reversal of the burden of proof from owner to claimant, is where the marks actually are. The third is writing limb b) as a four-line glossary when it carries eight of the sixteen marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the LLMC question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Limb a): 1 what the Convention is and the bargain it strikes; 2 its purpose; 3 the two heads of claim; 4 who may limit and what Article 3 excepts. Limb b): 5 plaintiff and defendant; 6 privity, and why it is the old test; 7 unlimited liability and the three routes to it. The printed marks are 8 and 8, so limb b) gets three real sections.
retrieval_cards.why: Writing limb b) as a short glossary throws away half the marks, and it is the commonest structural failure on this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the two heads of claims for which limitation is stated, and what about passengers?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under Article 6 the two heads are claims for loss of life or personal injury, and any other claims - in practice property damage and consequential loss. Each has its own fund calculated on tonnage, and the life fund is the larger; if it is exhausted the unsatisfied balance ranks rateably against the property fund. Passenger claims are NOT one of the two heads - they have a separate limit under Article 7.
retrieval_cards.why: Offering passengers as one of the two heads is the single most common way candidates lose this limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who can limit liability under the LLMC?
retrieval_cards.answer: Shipowners and salvors under Article 1. 'Shipowner' is defined to mean the owner, charterer, manager and operator of a seagoing ship. A salvor is anyone rendering services in direct connexion with salvage operations. The right extends to any person for whose act, neglect or default the shipowner or salvor is responsible, including master and crew, and to the insurer of liability to the same extent as the assured.
retrieval_cards.why: Answering only 'the shipowner' misses four of the five categories, and the insurer point is what makes the cap commercially real.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define privity, and say why it belongs to the old test.
retrieval_cards.answer: Privity means knowledge and concurrence - the owner knew of the fault or state of affairs and assented to it. It is knowledge plus acquiescence, personal to the owner or his directing mind. Under the 1957 Convention the limit broke on the owner's 'actual fault or privity', and the OWNER bore the burden of disproving it. Article 4 of the LLMC 1976 replaced that test entirely.
retrieval_cards.why: Presenting privity as the current test loses the whole point of the section, which is the displacement.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What replaced the 'actual fault or privity' test, and why does it matter so much?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 4 of the LLMC 1976: the limit is broken only where the loss resulted from the person's personal act or omission, committed with intent to cause such loss, or recklessly and with knowledge that such loss would probably result. Two things changed at once - the standard rose from fault to intent or informed recklessness, and the burden moved from the owner to the claimant. That reversal is why the modern right is described as virtually unbreakable.
retrieval_cards.why: The burden reversal is the analytical high point of limb b) and the most quotable single fact on the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the three routes to unlimited liability.
retrieval_cards.answer: One, the Article 4 conduct is proved - intent, or recklessness with knowledge that such loss would probably result. Two, the claim is an Article 3 excepted claim - salvage, general average contribution, CLC oil pollution, nuclear damage, certain employee claims - so it was never inside the Convention. Three, the Convention does not apply at all: the forum State is not a party, the person is not entitled to limit, or the fund is not constituted.
retrieval_cards.why: Most candidates give only route one, and setting out three is what turns a definition into an answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does maritime law allow a party at fault to cap his liability at all?
retrieval_cards.answer: Principally insurability: a liability with a calculable ceiling can be underwritten, one without a ceiling cannot be priced. Without a cap there is no liability market, and a claimant's judgment is then worth only what a single-ship company owns. It also gives certainty and finality before the casualty, encourages a hazardous venture conducted far from the owner's supervision, and provides an orderly rateable distribution rather than a race between jurisdictions.
retrieval_cards.why: It turns the purpose limb from a recital into an argument, and it explains why losing the right is catastrophic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian statute gives effect to limitation of liability at an October 2023 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Part XA of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. The Merchant Shipping Act 2025 did not commence until 15 March 2026, roughly two and a half years after this sitting, and must not be cited here. No monetary limit or Special Drawing Right figure should be quoted either, since the applicable figures depend on which Protocol and amendment the State concerned has adopted.
retrieval_cards.why: The 1958 Act is the standing statute trap for the whole 2023 batch, and this is a legal question where the temptation is greatest.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two limbs printed at eight marks each. Limb a) contains THREE distinct questions - what the LLMC is and its purpose, the two heads of claims, and who can limit - and each must be visibly answered rather than blended. Limb b) is a definitions limb, but at eight marks it is not a glossary: the examiner is testing whether the candidate understands that PRIVITY belongs to a superseded test and that UNLIMITED LIABILITY has more than one route to it. At management level the question is really testing whether the candidate grasps why the law permits a cap at all, which is insurability.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: Printed, complete and internally consistent: a) (8) and b) (8), summing to sixteen. The route therefore gives FOUR steps to limb a) - because it asks three separate questions and the purpose deserves its own section - and THREE to limb b). Note the contrast with the same question at the January 2023 sitting, which printed no marks at all: here the equal weighting of the two limbs is EVIDENCED rather than inferred, which is a positive reason to give limb b) full sections.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: For a): the Convention correctly named and dated, the Protocol and its 2012 amendments, the Indian vehicle, the tonnage-based cap and the near-automatic / near-unbreakable bargain; a purpose section that reaches insurability rather than stopping at 'to protect shipowners'; the two heads correctly stated under Article 6 with passengers correctly excluded to Article 7; and a full account of who may limit, including the insurer, together with the Article 3 exceptions. For b): plaintiff and defendant with the burden of proof identified and the procedural inversion noted; privity correctly defined as knowledge and concurrence AND correctly placed as the superseded test, with the Article 4 replacement and the burden reversal explained; and unlimited liability with all three routes and the insurability consequence.

blocks.h: 1. The background - the gap the Convention was written to close

blocks.p: The international oil pollution compensation regime was built in response to tanker casualties, and it was shaped accordingly. The Civil Liability Convention attaches to persistent oil carried as cargo in bulk by a tanker, together with the bunkers carried by such a ship. Anything outside that description simply fell outside the regime.

The gap that leaves is obvious once stated. A large container ship or bulk carrier carries no oil cargo at all - but she carries her own fuel, and on a modern ship that may amount to thousands of tonnes of heavy fuel oil in tanks along her sides. If she grounds, that oil causes the same contamination on the same coastline as a cargo spill would. Until 2008 the people affected had to fall back on ordinary national law: identify a defendant, prove fault against him, and then find assets within a jurisdiction where a judgment could actually be enforced. Against a single-ship company registered elsewhere, that is frequently worthless.
The International Convention on Civil Liability for Bunker Oil Pollution Damage, 2001 was adopted on 23 March 2001 and entered into force on 21 November 2008 to close that gap.

blocks.h: 2. Its relevance - where it sits in the liability architecture

blocks.p: Its relevance is that it completes the pollution-liability map for the world fleet. Tankers were already covered for cargo oil; every other ship is now covered for her fuel. To do that it borrows the three mechanisms the tanker regime had already proved:

ul: Strict liability. The shipowner is liable for pollution damage caused by bunker oil on board or originating from the ship, and the claimant does not have to prove negligence - only the escape and the resulting damage.
Compulsory insurance or other financial security, evidenced by a certificate that must be carried on board and which is checkable by port State control.
Direct action against the insurer. The claimant may bring his claim against the provider of the financial security, so an insolvent or evasive owner does not defeat the claim.

blocks.p: But its relevance must be stated with its limitation, because that limitation is what the last part of the question turns on: the Convention has no limit of its own - it preserves the shipowner's right to limit under whatever regime applies, in practice the LLMC - and there is no compensation fund standing behind it. Its practical achievement is therefore certainty of recovery rather than size of recovery: it makes it far more likely that there is somebody solvent to sue, without increasing the total sum ultimately available.

Definition. Pollution damage means loss or damage caused outside the ship by contamination resulting from the escape or discharge of bunker oil from the ship, wherever such escape or discharge may occur, subject to two qualifications: compensation for impairment of the environment, other than loss of profit flowing from that impairment, is limited to the costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken; and the definition includes the costs of preventive measures and any further loss or damage caused by those measures. Preventive measures are in turn any reasonable measures taken by any person after an incident to prevent or minimise pollution damage.

Two features are worth drawing out. The words outside the ship exclude damage to the ship herself and to her equipment - that is the owner's own loss, not pollution damage. And the reinstatement qualification is a deliberate policy choice: it prevents speculative claims for abstract environmental harm while allowing the real cost of cleaning up and restoring.

Difference from CLC 92: the formula is essentially the same. This definition is modelled directly on the CLC definition and carries the same reinstatement limitation and the same inclusion of preventive measures. The difference between the two regimes is not in what counts as damage but in what oil the definition attaches to - which is the next item.
Definition. Bunker oil means any hydrocarbon mineral oil, including lubricating oil, used or intended to be used for the operation or propulsion of the ship, and any residues of such oil.
Three points inside that definition earn marks:

ul: It expressly includes lubricating oil, which is easily forgotten and is not intuitive - most candidates think only of fuel.
It includes residues, so sludge, tank washings and the contents of the sludge tank are within it.
It is NOT confined to persistent oil. A distillate or gas oil bunker is bunker oil for the purposes of this Convention.

blocks.p: Difference from CLC 92 - and this is the sharpest of the four. CLC attaches to persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil carried as cargo in bulk aboard a ship constructed or adapted to carry oil in bulk as cargo, together with such a ship's bunkers. The two regimes are therefore distinguished by the character and the role of the oil: persistent, and carried as cargo, against any hydrocarbon mineral oil, carried as fuel. Consistently with that, the 'ship' to which the Bunker Convention applies is defined very widely - any seagoing vessel and seaborne craft, of any type whatsoever.

Definition. Rights to compensation under the Convention are extinguished unless an action is brought within three years from the date on which the damage occurred. In addition, no action may in any case be brought after six years from the date of the incident which caused the damage. Where the incident consists of a series of occurrences, the six-year period runs from the date of the first of them.

The two periods are worth distinguishing properly because they run from different events. The three-year period runs from the damage; the six-year period runs from the incident. Where damage emerges slowly - contamination discovered long after a grounding - the six-year long stop can therefore cut short a three-year period that would otherwise still be open. And the series-of-occurrences rule prevents a claimant extending the long stop by pointing at the last event in a chain rather than the first.

Difference from CLC 92: none of substance. CLC 92 imposes the same three-year and six-year structure, running from the same two events, with the same rule for a series of occurrences. The Bunker Convention deliberately mirrors it so that a claimant does not face two different clocks depending on which regime turns out to apply. Saying plainly that this item is the same is worth a mark, because it shows the comparison was actually made rather than assumed.
The exclusions from scope are these:

ul: CLC damage is excluded. The Convention does not apply to pollution damage as defined in the CLC, whether or not compensation is payable in respect of it under that Convention. This is the most important exclusion: it makes the two regimes mutually exclusive rather than cumulative, so there is no double recovery and no gap of overlap.
Warships, naval auxiliaries and other ships owned or operated by a State and used, for the time being, only on government non-commercial service are excluded.
A State Party may nevertheless decide to apply the Convention to such ships, and may extend it to ships not otherwise covered - so the exclusion is a default rather than an absolute.

blocks.p: A distinction must be drawn here, because the printed item invites it to be blurred: EXCLUSIONS from scope are not the same as DEFENCES to liability. The shipowner also has defences, and they operate quite differently - the Convention applies, but liability does not attach. They are: that the damage resulted from an act of war, hostilities, civil war, insurrection, or a natural phenomenon of an exceptional, inevitable and irresistible character; that it was wholly caused by an act or omission done with intent to cause damage by a third party; and that it was wholly caused by the negligence or other wrongful act of a government or authority responsible for the maintenance of lights or other navigational aids. In addition, contributory negligence on the part of the person suffering the damage may reduce or wholly exonerate the shipowner as against that person.
Difference from CLC 92: the exclusions and the defences closely mirror those in CLC. The genuine divergence between the two regimes lies elsewhere, and it is the subject of the final section.

blocks.h: 7. The differences taken together - who, limit, fund, threshold

blocks.p: Taken as a whole, the two Conventions differ in four ways that matter, and the four are best held as WHO - LIMIT - FUND - THRESHOLD.

rows: Who is liable
A WIDE 'shipowner' - owner including registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator - JOINTLY AND SEVERALLY
EXCLUSIVELY CHANNELLED to the REGISTERED OWNER, with claims against a listed group expressly barred
The limit
NO free-standing limit; expressly preserves the right to limit under any applicable regime, in practice the LLMC as amended
Its OWN limit, calculated on the ship's tonnage under Article V
A fund behind it
NONE. When the limitation fund is exhausted, that is the end
The 1992 Fund Convention and the 2003 Supplementary Fund Protocol - a second and third tier
Insurance threshold
By GROSS TONNAGE - ships above 1,000 gross tonnage
By CARGO - ships carrying more than 2,000 tonnes of persistent oil in bulk as cargo
The oil
Any hydrocarbon mineral oil used as fuel, including lubricating oil and residues; NOT confined to persistent oil
Persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil carried as CARGO in bulk, plus such a ship's bunkers
Time limits
Three years from damage, six-year long stop from the incident
The SAME - three years and a six-year long stop

blocks.p: The first two rows deserve comment because they are the most instructive. The two Conventions solve the same problem in opposite directions. CLC decided that a claimant's difficulty was not knowing whom to sue, and answered it by channelling liability onto one certain, identifiable party - the registered owner - and then standing two international funds behind him. The Bunker Convention decided that a claimant's difficulty was finding somebody solvent to sue, and answered it by making a wide group of commercial parties jointly and severally liable, so that if the registered owner is a shell company the manager, operator or bareboat charterer remains answerable.

The consequence for a claimant is worth stating explicitly as the conclusion of the answer. Under the Bunker Convention there are more defendants but a lower ceiling and no fund; under CLC there is one defendant but three tiers of compensation behind him. In a very large bunker spill from a big ship, the compensation available may therefore prove materially less than would be available for a comparable cargo spill from a tanker - which is a known and deliberate feature of the architecture, and is a point of continuing debate rather than an oversight.

The stem prints four items and gives them no separate marks, so they carry comparable weight and each must be genuinely defined and genuinely compared - the instruction is 'define the following... and explain how they differ'. A candidate who defines all four and never compares has answered half the question. The two framing sections at the front are what let the comparison make sense, and the closing comparison section is where the real analysis lives, because the biggest differences between the two regimes are not in the four printed items at all - they are in who is liable, whose limit applies, whether there is a fund, and what triggers compulsory insurance.

blocks.h: The idea that makes the Convention explicable

blocks.p: The old regime was built for tanker cargo. A container ship carries no oil cargo but carries thousands of tonnes of her own fuel, which does identical damage. That gap - and the fact that filling it meant falling back on national law, with all its problems of proof and enforcement - is the entire background limb, and it can be written in three sentences.

blocks.h: The honest summary to close on

blocks.p: The Bunker Convention improves the certainty of recovery, not the size of it. It gives the claimant strict liability, a wide range of defendants, compulsory insurance and direct action - so there is almost always somebody solvent to sue. But it has no limit of its own and no fund behind it, so the total available is bounded by the limitation regime alone. Making that point turns a list of differences into an assessment.

ul: Defining bunker oil as fuel oil. It is any hydrocarbon mineral oil used or intended for operation or propulsion, expressly including lubricating oil, and including residues - and it is not confined to persistent oil.
Saying the time limits differ from CLC. They do not. Saying so plainly is worth a mark; inventing a difference costs one.

Confusing exclusions from scope with defences to liability. Different provisions, different effect - one means the Convention does not apply at all, the other means it applies but liability does not attach.
Forgetting that CLC damage is excluded - the provision that stops the two regimes overlapping.
Saying the Bunker Convention has its own limit. It does not. It borrows the LLMC's.
Forgetting that there is no fund behind the Bunker Convention. It is the most practically important difference of all.
Quoting monetary limits or fund ceilings. They depend on the amendments in force for the State concerned.

Channelling versus joint and several liability. CLC channels exclusively to the registered owner and bars claims against a listed group; the Bunker Convention makes owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator jointly and severally liable. The two Conventions solve the same problem in opposite directions, and saying so is the analytical high point of the answer.
The insurance threshold is measured differently. Bunker by gross tonnage; CLC by cargo carried. Candidates routinely give both as tonnage.
'Outside the ship' in the pollution damage definition excludes damage to the ship herself. Cheap and precise.
The three-year and six-year periods run from different events - damage, and incident - which is why the long stop can cut short an otherwise live claim.
The series-of-occurrences rule runs the six years from the FIRST occurrence, not the last.
Do not import later law. At this sitting the domestic vehicle is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958; the 2025 Act did not commence until 15 March 2026.
Why was the Bunker Convention needed? - CLC covered only persistent oil carried as cargo by a tanker; a non-tanker's own bunkers, which may be thousands of tonnes, fell outside the regime entirely.
When did it enter force? - adopted 23 March 2001, in force 21 November 2008.
Define bunker oil. - any hydrocarbon mineral oil, including lubricating oil, used or intended to be used for the operation or propulsion of the ship, and any residues of such oil.
Is a gas oil bunker covered? - yes. Unlike CLC, the definition is not confined to persistent oil.
Who can be sued? - the shipowner widely defined: owner including registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator, jointly and severally; and the insurer, by direct action.
How does that differ from CLC? - CLC channels liability exclusively to the registered owner and bars claims against a listed group including charterers, managers, salvors and crew.
What limits the shipowner's liability? - not this Convention. It preserves the right to limit under the applicable regime, in practice the LLMC as amended.
Is there a fund? - no. That is the most important practical difference from CLC, which has the 1992 Fund and the 2003 Supplementary Fund behind it.
What are the time limits? - three years from the date the damage occurred, and a six-year long stop from the incident; where the incident is a series of occurrences, the six years run from the first.
Which ships must carry insurance? - under the Bunker Convention, those above 1,000 gross tonnage. Under CLC, those carrying more than 2,000 tonnes of persistent oil in bulk as cargo.

blocks.p: GAP - PLACE - P, B, T, E - COMPARE. The four printed definitions run in the printed order: Pollution damage, Bunker oil, Time limits, Exclusions. Then the closing comparison is WHO - LIMIT - FUND - THRESHOLD. Inside each definition section, define first and compare second, so the examiner can see both halves of his instruction being obeyed.

ul: Bunker Convention 2001, Article 1 - definitions: shipowner, ship, bunker oil, incident, preventive measures, pollution damage.
Article 3 - liability of the shipowner; strict liability, the defences, and joint and several liability.
Article 4 - exclusions, including CLC damage and State ships on non-commercial service.
Article 6 - limitation of liability. It preserves the right to limit under other regimes and creates none of its own.
Article 7 - compulsory insurance, the certificate, and direct action; the threshold is by gross tonnage.
Article 8 - time limits: three years and a six-year long stop. Articles 9 and 10 - jurisdiction, recognition and enforcement.
CLC 92, Articles I, II, III, V, VII and VIII - definitions, scope, exclusive channelling, its own limit, compulsory insurance by cargo carried, and time limits.
1992 Fund Convention and 2003 Supplementary Fund Protocol - the second and third tiers behind CLC. No counterpart behind the Bunker Convention.
LLMC 1976 as amended by the 1996 Protocol - the regime from which the Bunker Convention borrows its ceiling.
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (India) - the domestic vehicle in force at this sitting.

blocks.p: Four limits are recorded. First, no Convention text is quoted verbatim anywhere in this answer; all four definitions are given in substance at corpus identity level. Second, no monetary limit, tonnage-based fund figure or Fund ceiling is asserted. The Bunker Convention borrows its ceiling from the applicable limitation regime, so the figure depends on which Protocol and amendment the State concerned has adopted, and the CLC and Fund figures likewise depend on the amendments in force for that State; neither Convention text was read this session. Third, the Indian domestic vehicle is identified as the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 without asserting a ratification instrument, accession date or statutory part not read this session - and the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 commenced 15 March 2026, roughly two and a half years after this sitting, and is excluded. Fourth, the account of the defences under Article 3 is given in substance and is expressly distinguished from the exclusions from scope under Article 4; no judicial authority on the construction of either provision was read. On currency, nothing in either Convention moved between this sitting and either of the family sittings against which it was checked - the closely related April 2023 question six months earlier, and the identical question at the February 2024 sitting four months later.

questions.understand_first: There is a gap in the story that this Convention was written to fill, and if you can see the gap the whole answer follows. When the international community first built a compensation regime for oil pollution, it was reacting to tanker casualties - a laden tanker breaking up and covering a coastline in cargo oil. So the regime it built was aimed precisely at that: persistent oil, carried as cargo, in bulk, by a tanker. Anything outside that description was simply not covered by it. Which leaves an obvious problem. A large container ship or bulk carrier carries no oil cargo at all - but she carries her own fuel, and on a modern ship that can run to thousands of tonnes of heavy oil sitting in tanks along her sides. If she grounds, that fuel does exactly the same damage to exactly the same coastline, and for decades the people whose beaches and fishing grounds were ruined had to fall back on ordinary national law: work out who to sue, prove they were negligent, and then hope the company that owned the ship had assets somewhere they could reach. That is a bad answer, and the Bunker Convention is the correction. It takes the machinery the tanker regime had already proved - you are liable whether or not you were careless; you must carry insurance; and the victim can sue the insurer directly - and applies it to bunkers. But it does not copy the tanker regime wholesale, and the differences are what the last part of the question is really about. The tanker regime funnels liability onto one named party and then stands a large international fund behind him. This Convention does the opposite on the first point - it makes a whole group of people liable together, so there is almost always somebody to sue - and it simply omits the second: there is no fund. It also has no ceiling of its own; it borrows one from the general limitation convention. So the honest summary is that it improves your chance of finding someone who can pay, without improving how much is ultimately available.
