Borrows the proved machinery - STRICT LIABILITY (no need to prove negligence), COMPULSORY INSURANCE with a certificate (PSC-checkable), DIRECT ACTION against the insurer. BUT no limit of its own and NO FUND - so it improves certainty of recovery, not size of recovery. (a) POLLUTION DAMAGE. Loss or damage caused OUTSIDE the ship by contamination from escape or discharge of bunker oil, wherever it occurs; environmental impairment other than loss of profit limited to costs of REASONABLE MEASURES OF REINSTATEMENT actually undertaken or to be undertaken; includes cost of PREVENTIVE MEASURES and further loss caused by them. vs CLC: SAME FORMULA - the difference is what oil it attaches to. (b) BUNKER OIL. Any hydrocarbon mineral oil, INCLUDING LUBRICATING OIL, used or intended for the operation or propulsion of the ship, and any RESIDUES. NOT confined to PERSISTENT oil. vs CLC: the sharpest difference - CLC is persistent oil carried as CARGO in bulk. Character and role of the oil. Bunker 'ship' = any seagoing vessel and seaborne craft of any type whatsoever. (c) TIME LIMITS. THREE YEARS from the date the damage occurred; SIX-YEAR long stop from the date of the INCIDENT; series of occurrences - six years run from the FIRST. Two different clocks from two different events, so the long stop can cut short a live three-year claim. vs CLC: THE SAME - say so plainly, it earns the mark. (d) EXCLUSIONS. CLC damage excluded, whether or not compensation is payable under CLC - makes the regimes mutually exclusive. Warships, naval auxiliaries, State ships on government non-commercial service; a State may nevertheless apply it to them, and may extend it. DISTINGUISH DEFENCES (Art 3) - war, hostilities, civil war, insurrection, exceptional inevitable irresistible natural phenomenon; wholly caused by a third party's act done with intent; wholly caused by negligence of an authority maintaining navigational aids; plus contributory negligence. vs CLC: closely mirrored. THE FOUR REAL DIFFERENCES - WHO, LIMIT, FUND, THRESHOLD. WHO: Bunker = WIDE shipowner - owner incl. registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager, operator - JOINTLY AND SEVERALLY. CLC = EXCLUSIVE CHANNELLING to the REGISTERED OWNER, claims against a listed group barred. Opposite solutions to the same problem - Bunker gives MORE defendants, CLC gives ONE CERTAIN defendant. LIMIT: Bunker has NONE of its own, borrows the LLMC; CLC has its own tonnage limit. FUND: Bunker NONE; CLC has the 1992 Fund and the 2003 Supplementary Fund - three tiers. THRESHOLD: Bunker by GROSS TONNAGE, above 1,000 GT; CLC by CARGO, more than 2,000 tonnes of persistent oil in bulk. Conclusion: more defendants, lower ceiling, no fund - so a large bunker spill may attract materially less compensation than a comparable cargo spill.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: Bunker Convention 2001, Article 1 carries the definitions of bunker oil and pollution damage; Article 3 the strict liability of a WIDELY DEFINED shipowner - owner including registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator, jointly and severally - together with the defences; Article 4 the exclusions, of which the most important is that CLC damage is excluded whether or not compensation is payable under CLC; Article 6 which preserves the right to limit under other regimes and creates no limit of its own; Article 7 compulsory insurance above 1,000 gross tonnage with direct action; and Article 8 the three-year period and six-year long stop. Against it, CLC 92 Article III channels liability exclusively to the registered owner, Article V sets its own tonnage limit, Article VII triggers insurance by cargo carried, and Article VIII imposes the same time limits. The 1992 Fund Convention and 2003 Supplementary Fund Protocol stand behind CLC and have no counterpart behind the Bunker Convention.
quick_revision.major_trap: Defining bunker oil too narrowly. It is any hydrocarbon mineral oil used or intended for the operation or propulsion of the ship, expressly including lubricating oil, and including residues - and unlike CLC it is not confined to persistent oil. The second trap is inventing a difference in the time limits: they are the same three-year and six-year structure as CLC 92, and saying so plainly earns the mark that inventing a difference loses. The third is blurring exclusions from scope with defences to liability - the first means the Convention does not apply, the second that it applies but liability does not attach. And the fourth is missing the two differences that matter most: the Bunker Convention has no limit of its own, borrowing the LLMC's, and no fund behind it at all.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the Bunker Convention question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 the background and the gap; 2 its relevance and place in the architecture; 3 (a) pollution damage; 4 (b) bunker oil; 5 (c) time limits; 6 (d) exclusions; 7 the differences taken together - who, limit, fund, threshold. Inside each of steps 3 to 6, define first and compare with CLC second, because the stem asks for both.
retrieval_cards.why: The four printed items run in printed order, and the biggest differences from CLC are not in those items at all - they are in step 7.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define bunker oil under the Bunker Convention, and say how it differs from CLC's oil.
retrieval_cards.answer: Any hydrocarbon mineral oil, including lubricating oil, used or intended to be used for the operation or propulsion of the ship, and any residues of such oil. It expressly includes lubricating oil and residues and is NOT confined to persistent oil. CLC by contrast attaches to persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil carried as CARGO in bulk, plus such a ship's bunkers. The distinction is the character and the role of the oil.
retrieval_cards.why: The sharpest of the four printed comparisons, and the one candidates most often define too narrowly.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define pollution damage under the Bunker Convention.
retrieval_cards.answer: Loss or damage caused OUTSIDE the ship by contamination resulting from the escape or discharge of bunker oil from the ship, wherever it occurs; with compensation for environmental impairment other than loss of profit limited to the costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken; and including the costs of preventive measures and further loss caused by them. The formula is essentially the same as CLC's.
retrieval_cards.why: 'Outside the ship' and the reinstatement limitation are the two precise points inside a long definition.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the time limits, and say whether they differ from CLC 92.
retrieval_cards.answer: Three years from the date on which the damage occurred, and in no case more than six years from the date of the incident which caused the damage; where the incident consists of a series of occurrences, the six years run from the first of them. They do NOT differ from CLC 92, which imposes the same structure from the same two events. Saying so plainly is worth a mark.
retrieval_cards.why: Inventing a difference here is a common and entirely avoidable loss.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the exclusions from the defences under the Bunker Convention.
retrieval_cards.answer: Exclusions go to scope: CLC damage is excluded whether or not compensation is payable under CLC, and warships and State ships on government non-commercial service are excluded, though a State may apply it to them. Defences go to liability: war, hostilities, civil war, insurrection or an exceptional, inevitable and irresistible natural phenomenon; damage wholly caused by a third party's act done with intent; damage wholly caused by an authority's negligence in maintaining navigational aids; plus contributory negligence.
retrieval_cards.why: The printed item (d) invites the two to be blurred, and keeping them apart is where the marks are.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do the Bunker Convention and CLC 92 differ on WHO is liable?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Bunker Convention defines shipowner widely - owner including the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator - and makes them jointly and severally liable. CLC 92 does the opposite: it channels liability exclusively to the registered owner and expressly bars claims against a listed group including charterers, managers, salvors and crew. The two solve the same problem in opposite directions - more defendants against one certain defendant.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the analytical high point of the answer and it explains the design of both regimes at once.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What limits liability under the Bunker Convention, and what fund stands behind it?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Convention creates NO limit of its own - it expressly preserves the right to limit under any applicable national or international regime, in practice the LLMC as amended. And NO fund stands behind it at all: when the limitation fund is exhausted, that is the end. CLC by contrast has its own tonnage-based limit and is backed by the 1992 Fund Convention and the 2003 Supplementary Fund Protocol.
retrieval_cards.why: The absence of a fund is the most practically important difference between the two regimes and the most often forgotten.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Compare the compulsory insurance thresholds of the two Conventions.
retrieval_cards.answer: The Bunker Convention requires insurance or other financial security for ships above 1,000 gross tonnage - a threshold measured by the SIZE of the ship. CLC 92 requires it for ships carrying more than 2,000 tonnes of persistent oil in bulk as cargo - a threshold measured by the CARGO. Candidates routinely give both as tonnage thresholds, which loses the distinction.
retrieval_cards.why: A precise, cheap mark that also demonstrates the different logic of the two regimes.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Sum up what the Bunker Convention achieved and what it did not.
retrieval_cards.answer: It improved the CERTAINTY of recovery, not the SIZE of it. Strict liability, a wide group of jointly and severally liable defendants, compulsory insurance and direct action against the insurer mean there is almost always somebody solvent to sue. But with no limit of its own and no fund behind it, the total available is bounded by the limitation regime alone - so a large bunker spill may attract materially less compensation than a comparable tanker cargo spill.
retrieval_cards.why: It turns a list of differences into an assessment, which is what a management-level answer is for.

blocks.h: 1. a) What root cause analysis is, and why it is required

blocks.p: Root cause analysis is a structured method for establishing the underlying organisational reasons why an event occurred, as distinct from identifying the immediate failure that preceded it. Its purpose is stated most usefully in negative form: it exists to prevent recurrence, not to establish what went wrong on the day and certainly not to establish who was responsible.

The obligation to do it arises from two directions. Externally, the Casualty Investigation Code, resolution MSC.255(84) of 2008, has had Parts I and II mandatory through SOLAS regulation XI-1/6 since 1 January 2010, and requires a marine safety investigation into every very serious marine casualty - the total loss of a ship, loss of life, or severe damage to the environment. Critically, the Code separates the safety investigation from any investigation that apportions blame or liability, and that separation is not a technicality: it is what makes root cause analysis possible at all, because people will not describe their own errors honestly to an investigation that can punish them.

Internally, the ISM Code regulation 9 requires the safety management system to include procedures ensuring that non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences are reported to the Company, investigated and analysed, with the objective of improving safety, and that the Company establishes procedures for corrective action. Regulation 1.2.2 requires the assessment of all identified risks and the establishment of appropriate safeguards, and regulation 12 supplies the verification, review and evaluation machinery. So the discipline is required of the flag State after a casualty and of the Company continuously.

blocks.h: 2. a) The principles of root cause analysis

ul: Seek causes, not culprits. The moment the investigation becomes an inquiry into who is to blame, the information stops arriving.
Every accident has multiple causes. A finding with a single cause is an incomplete investigation, not a simple accident.
Go beyond the immediate. Keep asking why until you reach something the organisation controls and can change.
Base findings on evidence, and gather perishable evidence first - memories, volatile records and physical conditions all degrade.
Establish the sequence before attempting the explanation. Analysis performed before the timeline is settled fits the facts to a theory.
Test each causal factor by removal. If the outcome would have occurred anyway without it, it is not causal.
A root cause must be ACTIONABLE. This is the most useful single test in the method - and it is why 'human error' is never a root cause. You cannot write a corrective action against it.
Correct at the level at which the cause sits. A systemic cause cannot be corrected by retraining one individual.
Close the loop. Verify both that the action was implemented and that it was effective - two different checks - and share the lesson across the fleet.
Just culture. Honest reporting must be safe, or the raw material on which the whole method depends never arrives.

blocks.h: 3. a) The steps of a root cause analysis

ul: Recognise and report - and make the situation safe first. No investigation begins while the casualty is still developing.

Preserve and collect evidence - voyage and engine data recorders, alarm and event logs, planned maintenance and defect records, work and rest hour records, permits to work, risk assessments, drawings and manuals, and above all early witness accounts, taken before recollection is contaminated by discussion.
Establish the sequence of events - a timeline, or more formally an event and causal factor chart, so that what happened is settled before why it happened is debated.
Identify the causal factors and test each by removal.

Analyse to root cause using an appropriate technique - five whys for a simple chain, a fishbone or cause-and-effect diagram to organise contributory factors, a fault tree for a complex technical event, or barrier analysis where the question is which defence failed.
Identify the failed defences and how they failed - absent, inadequate, bypassed or unmaintained are four different findings requiring four different responses.
Develop corrective and preventive action - corrective to fix what happened, preventive to stop the class of event - each with a named owner and a date.
Implement and verify. Two checks: that the action was implemented, and that it was effective. The second is routinely skipped and its omission is why the same finding recurs.
Communicate the lesson fleet-wide and feed it back into risk assessment, procedures, training, the planned maintenance system and the management review.

blocks.h: 4. a) Proximate cause versus root cause

blocks.p: The proximate cause is the event directly preceding the outcome. It sits at the sharp end, it is immediate in time, and it is nearly always obvious - which is exactly why investigations stop there. The root cause is the underlying systemic reason the proximate cause was able to occur and to have that consequence. It sits at the blunt end, is often years earlier and far from the ship, and is rarely obvious at all.
The difference is best stated in one sentence: correcting the proximate cause restores the situation; correcting the root cause prevents recurrence.

A worked example. A lubricating oil pump bearing seizes. The proximate cause is that the pump ran without a suction supply. Ask why, and the isolating valve was left shut after maintenance. Ask why, and the permit to work was closed out without the isolation being restored and checked. Ask why, and the permit close-out step required no independent signature. Ask why, and the permit procedure was a generic company document never reviewed against this ship's actual systems. That last item is a root cause: it is something the organisation controls, and it is actionable. Correcting the proximate cause replaces a bearing. Correcting the root cause revises the permit system across the fleet - and prevents the next event, which would not have been a bearing at all.
A quick test keeps the two apart in the examination room: if the recommendation is 'replace it and remind the crew', you have found the proximate cause and stopped.

One distinction should be noted to avoid confusion, because the same words appear elsewhere in the syllabus. In marine insurance, 'proximate cause' means the dominant or effective cause of a loss, for the purpose of deciding whether a peril insured against operated. It is a related idea but a different test, applied for a different purpose.
The two printed terms come out of a specific development in accident theory, and setting that out first is what makes them explicable rather than merely definable.

Sequential models came first. The best known is the domino model, in which an accident is the last of a line of falling dominoes and removing any one of them prevents the outcome. It is genuinely useful for conveying the idea of a causal chain, but it has a serious defect: it encourages the investigator to look for one removable cause close to the accident - which in practice means the last person who touched the equipment.

The organisational accident model replaced it. It pictures the system as a series of successive layers of defence - design, engineered safeguards, procedures, supervision, training, alarms, and finally the crew themselves. Each layer is imperfect and has holes in it; and crucially the holes move, opening and closing with workload, manning, fatigue, maintenance state and commercial pressure. An accident occurs only when the holes in every layer momentarily line up so that the hazard passes through all of them. This is popularly known as the Swiss cheese model.
Within that picture, failures divide according to where they originate and how quickly their effect appears - and that division is exactly what the two printed terms name.

Active failures are unsafe acts committed by people in direct contact with the system - the watchkeeper, the fitter, the officer of the watch - and their effects are felt almost immediately. They fall into three kinds, and giving the three with examples is what the limb asks for.

ul: Slips and lapses - skill-based failures in which the intention was correct and the execution or the memory was not. Example: an engineer opens the valve adjacent to the correct one, from habit, because the two are identical and side by side. He knew perfectly well which valve he wanted.

Mistakes - planning failures, in which the action was carried out exactly as intended but the plan itself was wrong. They may be rule-based, applying a good rule in the wrong situation, or knowledge-based, in a novel situation for which no rule exists. Example: an exhaust valve is burning; the temperature deviation is diagnosed as an instrument fault and the engine is kept at load.

Violations - deliberate departures from a known rule or procedure, which may be routine (the normal way the job is done here), situational (the rule cannot be complied with in these conditions) or exceptional (a departure in an emergency). Example: a permit to work signed retrospectively, because that is how it has always been done aboard.

blocks.p: Active failures are the most visible element in any accident, which is precisely why investigations stop at them. And one observation converts this section from description into analysis: a routine violation is diagnostic of a latent condition. If everybody does it, and has always done it, then the rule or the conditions in which people are asked to obey it are the problem - not the individual who was caught.

Latent failures are the delayed consequences of decisions taken by designers, builders, procedure writers, regulators and management. They are present in the system before the accident, often for years, and they lie dormant until combined with local triggers and an active failure. They act in two distinct ways: by creating error-provoking conditions in the workplace, and by creating long-lasting holes in the defences.

ul: Design. Poor ergonomics - identical adjacent valves with unclear labelling, controls that operate in an unnatural sense, instruments not visible from where the action is taken. This is the latent condition behind the slip in the previous section.
Procedure. Generic, unusable, absent or contradictory documentation - a checklist never revised for this installation, or a procedure so long that nobody reads it in practice.
Manning and resourcing. A manning level at which the rest-hour regime is arithmetically unachievable; deferred maintenance; a spares budget that turns a defect list into a permanent backlog.
Training. Familiarisation that certifies attendance rather than capability, so that the record shows a trained crew and the ship does not have one.
Maintenance management. Generic planned maintenance intervals never adjusted to this ship's actual duty, and a tolerated backlog of open defects.
Culture. Production pressure, discouraged reporting, near misses not investigated - the conditions under which the organisation stops finding out about itself.

blocks.p: The defining feature of a latent condition is that it causes nothing on its own. That is exactly why it survives for years, passes audits, and is invisible until the day it combines with an ordinary human error to produce a casualty.

blocks.h: 8. b) Why the distinction matters, and how the two combine

ul: Active failures are hard to prevent and easy to blame. People will always make slips; removing the individual who made this one leaves the next person in exactly the same conditions to make the same slip.

Latent conditions are the manageable target, and - decisively - they can be found proactively, before any accident, by audit, risk assessment, near-miss analysis and trend data. That is the entire justification for the ISM Code's audit, review and management-evaluation machinery.

An accident needs both. This is the point that explains everything else: it is why a trivial error causes nothing on a thousand ships and a catastrophe on the one where the defences had quietly rotted.

Because chance is real, outcome is a poor measure of behaviour. The same act can produce nothing, a near miss, or a fatality, depending on the state of defences the individual did not build and cannot see.

It follows that near misses must be investigated with the same rigour as accidents. They are free evidence about the state of the defences - the holes lined up far enough to be visible and then closed again.

Blame destroys the data. A just culture is not leniency: it distinguishes honest error, which is reported and learned from, from recklessness and wilful violation, which are not tolerated. Without that distinction the reports stop and the organisation goes blind.

blocks.p: The two halves of this question therefore join at a single point, and it is the right sentence to close on: root cause analysis is the technique that converts an active failure - a visible, individual, blameable act - into information about the latent conditions that made it likely and let it matter.

The stem sets four distinct tasks - principles, steps, the proximate-root distinction, and the two failure types with examples - and a candidate who merges any two of them loses marks by omission rather than by error. Principles and steps are not the same thing: principles are the rules the investigator obeys, steps are the sequence he follows, and answering one twice is the commonest structural failure here. Limb (b) explicitly says 'giving suitable examples', so examples are not decoration - they are instructed, and an answer without them cannot score full marks however accurate the definitions are.

This question prints no mark figure at all - neither a total nor a limb figure - and it is the only question on this paper that prints none. Under printed instruction 2 all questions carry equal marks, so it is worth sixteen like the rest. Treat the two limbs as eight and eight and divide your time accordingly; the same question at another sitting printed exactly that split.

blocks.h: The idea that makes the whole question explicable

blocks.p: A bad investigation stops at the last person to touch the equipment. The finding is nearly always true and nearly always useless, because the recommendation it produces is 'remind the crew to be careful' and six months later it happens again to somebody else. The whole subject is a discipline for not stopping there - for keeping going until you reach something the organisation controls and can change.

blocks.h: The one test that does most work

blocks.p: A root cause must be actionable. That single test disposes of 'human error', 'lack of attention' and 'failure to follow procedure' - you cannot write a corrective action against any of them. And it is the same test in reverse that identifies a proximate cause: if the recommendation is 'replace it and remind him', you have stopped at the sharp end.

ul: Merging principles with steps. They are different lists and the examiner asked for both.
Omitting examples in limb (b) when the stem instructs you to give them.
Defining a latent failure as 'a hidden fault'. It is a decision, taken elsewhere and earlier, whose consequence was delayed - not a fault that happened to be concealed.
Treating violations as simple misconduct. A routine violation is diagnostic of a latent condition and is one of the most valuable findings an investigation can make.
Forgetting the second verification. Checking that an action was implemented is not the same as checking that it was effective, and skipping the second is why findings recur.
Leaving out just culture. Without it the reports stop, and the method has nothing to work on.
Quoting a percentage of accidents attributable to human error. Those figures depend entirely on the classification methodology used.
The Casualty Investigation Code separates the safety investigation from blame and liability - and that separation is not administrative tidiness, it is what makes the method possible. Say why.
'Human error' is not a root cause. The single most quotable line in the answer.

The holes MOVE. Most candidates describe the Swiss cheese model as static layers with fixed holes. The whole insight is that the holes open and close with workload, manning, fatigue and maintenance state.
An accident needs both an active failure and latent conditions - which is why identical errors produce nothing on most ships.
Outcome is a poor measure of behaviour, and it is the argument for investigating near misses with equal rigour. They are free evidence.
Proximate cause means something different in marine insurance - the dominant or effective cause of a loss. Distinguishing the two shows range.
Do not import later law. At this sitting the Code is MSC.255(84), mandatory through SOLAS XI-1/6 since 1 January 2010, and the ISM Code as amended through MSC.353(92).
What is the purpose of a safety investigation? - prevention of recurrence, and expressly not the apportionment of blame or liability.
Which casualties must be investigated? - every very serious marine casualty: total loss, loss of life, or severe damage to the environment, under the Casualty Investigation Code and SOLAS XI-1/6.
Where does the Company's own obligation come from? - ISM Code regulation 9, with regulation 1.2.2 on risk assessment and regulation 12 on verification and review.

Give me the steps. - make safe, preserve evidence, establish the sequence, identify causal factors and test by removal, analyse to root cause, identify the failed defences, develop corrective and preventive action with owners and dates, implement and verify both implementation and effectiveness, and communicate fleet-wide.
Name three analytical techniques. - five whys, fishbone, fault tree, barrier analysis, event and causal factor charting.

Difference between proximate and root cause? - proximate is the event directly preceding the outcome at the sharp end; root is the systemic reason at the blunt end. Correcting the first restores the situation; correcting the second prevents recurrence.

Give an example of an active failure and of a latent failure that go together. - opening the identical adjacent valve from habit, against a design in which two identical valves sit side by side with unclear labelling.
What are the three kinds of active failure? - slips and lapses, mistakes, and violations.
Why is a routine violation important? - because if everybody does it, the rule or the conditions are wrong; it is diagnostic of a latent condition.
Why investigate near misses? - because outcome is a poor measure of behaviour, and a near miss is free evidence about the state of the defences.

blocks.p: Limb (a): COLLECT - SEQUENCE - CAUSAL FACTORS - ROOT - CORRECT AND VERIFY. Then SHARP END versus BLUNT END, NOW versus YEARS AGO. Limb (b): ACTIVE = who was there, felt at once. LATENT = who decided, felt much later. Hold the image of layers whose holes move, and close on the join: root cause analysis turns an active failure into information about latent conditions.

ul: Resolution MSC.255(84) - the Casualty Investigation Code, 2008. Parts I and II mandatory through SOLAS regulation XI-1/6 from 1 January 2010. Requires investigation of every very serious marine casualty, and separates the safety investigation from blame and liability.
SOLAS regulation XI-1/6 - investigations into marine casualties and incidents.
ISM Code regulation 9 - reports and analysis of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences, and corrective action. The Company's own obligation.
ISM Code regulation 1.2.2 - assessment of all identified risks and establishment of appropriate safeguards.
ISM Code regulation 12 - Company verification, review and evaluation. The machinery through which latent conditions are found proactively.
Resolution A.1070(28) - the IMO Instruments Implementation Code, on the flag State's casualty investigation obligations. Adopted 2013 and current at this sitting.
The accident causation models are academic theory, not instruments, and are not cited as such.

blocks.p: Four limits are recorded. First, no statistic or proportion is asserted anywhere - in particular no percentage attribution of marine accidents to human error. Such figures depend entirely on the classification methodology used and no primary source for any of them is held. Second, the worked examples are constructed illustrations and are presented as such; they are not reports of identified casualties, and no casualty investigation report was read this session. Third, the accident causation models are academic theory rather than instruments; they are described in substance and by their common names, with no author's text quoted and no publication cited. Fourth, the Casualty Investigation Code and ISM Code provisions are cited at corpus identity level and no Code text is reproduced verbatim. On currency, every instrument relied on was operative at this October 2023 sitting - the Code since 1 January 2010, the ISM Code as amended through MSC.353(92) since 1 January 2015, and the Instruments Implementation Code since 2013 - and none was superseded between this sitting and the later sitting against which the answer was checked.

questions.understand_first: Start with what goes wrong when an investigation is done badly, because that is what this whole subject is a correction for. Something happens - a pump seizes, a man is injured, oil goes over the side - and the investigation finds that somebody did something wrong. He opened the wrong valve, or he did not follow the procedure, or he was not paying attention. That finding is almost always true, and it is almost always useless, because it stops at the last person to touch the equipment and it produces a recommendation of the form 'remind the crew to be careful'. Six months later it happens again, to a different person. The reason it happens again is that the investigation stopped at the sharp end. The individual who made the error was working inside conditions somebody else created, sometimes years earlier and thousands of miles away - a valve that looks identical to its neighbour, a procedure written for a different ship, a manning level that makes the rest-hour rules arithmetically impossible, a maintenance budget that quietly turned a defect list into a backlog. Those conditions do not cause accidents by themselves; they sit there harmlessly for years. But they make certain errors much more likely, and when one finally happens they also mean the defences that should have caught it were not there. So the method in this question is a discipline for keeping going past the obvious answer until you reach something the organisation actually controls and can change. And the two terms in the second half are simply names for the two ends of that chain: the thing the person at the sharp end did, whose effect was felt immediately, and the thing the organisation decided long before, whose effect had been waiting. The single most useful idea to take away is that an accident needs both - which is why the same trivial error causes nothing on a thousand ships and a catastrophe on the one where the defences had quietly rotted.

steps.title: a) The principles of root cause analysis
points: Seek causes, not culprits

Establish the sequence before attempting the explanation
Test each causal factor by removal - would the outcome have changed without it?
A root cause must be ACTIONABLE. 'Human error' is not a root cause

Close the loop - verify implementation AND effectiveness, and share the lesson across the fleet
Just culture - honest reporting must be safe, or the raw material never arrives

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the root cause analysis question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Limb (a): 1 what RCA is and why it is required; 2 the principles; 3 the steps; 4 proximate versus root cause. Limb (b): 5 the accident causation models; 6 active failures with examples; 7 latent failures with examples; 8 why the distinction matters and how the two combine. Principles and steps are separate lists and both are asked for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is 'human error' never a root cause?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because a root cause must be ACTIONABLE - something the organisation controls and against which a corrective action can be written. 'Human error', 'lack of attention' and 'failure to follow procedure' are descriptions of the event, not explanations of it, and produce no corrective action beyond reminding people to be careful. The investigation has to keep going until it reaches a decision or a condition that can actually be changed.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the single most useful test in the method and the most quotable line in the answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Differentiate proximate cause from root cause, with a test.
retrieval_cards.answer: The proximate cause is the event directly preceding the outcome - at the sharp end, immediate in time, usually obvious. The root cause is the underlying systemic reason it could occur and matter - at the blunt end, often years earlier, rarely obvious. Correcting the proximate restores the situation; correcting the root prevents recurrence. The test: if the recommendation is 'replace it and remind him', you have stopped at the proximate cause.
retrieval_cards.why: The one-sentence difference and the practical test are what the limb is actually asking for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the steps of a root cause analysis.
retrieval_cards.answer: Recognise and report, making the situation safe first; preserve and collect evidence including early witness accounts; establish the sequence of events; identify causal factors and test each by removal; analyse to root cause using five whys, fishbone, fault tree or barrier analysis; identify the failed defences and how they failed; develop corrective and preventive action with owners and dates; implement and verify both implementation AND effectiveness; and communicate the lesson fleet-wide.
retrieval_cards.why: Two checks at the verification step, not one - skipping the effectiveness check is why findings recur.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define active failures and give the three kinds with an example of each.
retrieval_cards.answer: Unsafe acts by people in direct contact with the system, whose effects are felt almost immediately. Slips and lapses - skill-based, intention right and execution or memory wrong: opening the identical adjacent valve from habit. Mistakes - planning failures, rule-based or knowledge-based: diagnosing a burning exhaust valve as an instrument fault. Violations - deliberate departures, routine, situational or exceptional: a permit signed retrospectively.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem instructs that examples be given, so definitions alone cannot score full marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define latent failures and give examples.
retrieval_cards.answer: The delayed consequences of decisions by designers, builders, procedure writers, regulators and management, present in the system before the accident and dormant until combined with a local trigger. They create error-provoking conditions and long-lasting holes in the defences. Examples: identical adjacent valves poorly labelled; a checklist never revised for this installation; a manning level making rest hours unachievable; training that certifies attendance rather than capability; a tolerated defect backlog; a culture in which near misses are not reported.
retrieval_cards.why: A latent failure is a decision whose effect was delayed, not a fault that happened to be hidden.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the key insight of the organisational accident model that candidates usually miss?
retrieval_cards.answer: That the holes MOVE. The model pictures successive layers of defence - design, engineered safeguards, procedures, supervision, training, alarms, the crew - each with weaknesses; but those weaknesses open and close with workload, manning, fatigue, maintenance state and commercial pressure. An accident occurs only when the holes in every layer momentarily align. Describing the layers as static with fixed holes loses the whole point.
retrieval_cards.why: It is what separates a memorised diagram from an understanding of why accidents cluster in bad periods.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is a routine violation such a valuable finding?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because it is diagnostic of a latent condition rather than of an individual's character. If everybody departs from the rule, and always has, then either the rule cannot be complied with in the conditions people are given, or the procedure is unusable, or the manning and time available make compliance impossible. Disciplining the person who was caught leaves all of that untouched and guarantees recurrence.
retrieval_cards.why: It converts the violations paragraph from description into analysis.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why must near misses be investigated with the same rigour as accidents?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because chance is real and an accident needs both an active failure and aligned latent conditions, so outcome is a poor measure of behaviour - the same act may produce nothing, a near miss or a fatality depending on the state of defences the individual did not build. A near miss is free evidence: the holes lined up far enough to be visible and then closed again, at no cost.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the practical management conclusion the whole answer builds toward.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where do the obligations to investigate come from, and why does the separation from blame matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: Externally from the Casualty Investigation Code, resolution MSC.255(84), with Parts I and II mandatory through SOLAS XI-1/6 since 1 January 2010, requiring investigation of every very serious marine casualty. Internally from ISM Code regulation 9, with regulation 1.2.2 on risk assessment and regulation 12 on verification and review. The Code separates the safety investigation from blame and liability, and that separation is what makes root cause analysis possible - people do not describe their own errors honestly to an investigation that can punish them.
retrieval_cards.why: The separation is the structural point on which the whole method rests, and most candidates state it without explaining why it exists.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two limbs, each setting two tasks - so FOUR tasks in all, and each must be visibly answered. Limb (a) asks for the principles AND the steps of root cause analysis, which are two different lists, and then for a differentiation between proximate and root cause. Limb (b) asks for the two named failure types WITH EXAMPLES, which is an instruction rather than a suggestion. At management level the question is testing whether the candidate understands that the point of investigation is prevention rather than explanation, and that the manageable target is the organisation rather than the individual.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: PRINTED ANOMALY: this question prints NO mark figure at all, neither a total nor a limb figure, and is the only question on this paper to print none. It is recorded at 16 under printed instruction 2. The route treats the two limbs as of EQUAL WEIGHT, four steps each, and that assumption is corroborated from outside the paper: the same stem at another sitting prints (8) and (8). The absence of printed figures therefore costs the answer nothing.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: For (a): the purpose stated as prevention of recurrence; the regulatory basis in the Casualty Investigation Code and SOLAS XI-1/6 externally and the ISM Code internally, with the blame separation explained rather than merely stated; principles and steps given as two DISTINCT lists; and a differentiation of proximate from root that includes a worked example and the one-sentence statement of the difference. For (b): the causation models set out so the terms are explicable, then active failures divided into slips and lapses, mistakes and violations WITH EXAMPLES, latent failures given by category WITH EXAMPLES, and a closing section explaining why latent conditions are the manageable target and why an accident requires both.

The human-factors theory is academic literature and does not move with the sitting at all. The residual risk is simply that this is the LONGEST donor distance on the paper at fourteen months, so the forward check was run in full rather than assumed.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The Casualty Investigation Code and the ISM Code are of general application through SOLAS. Where a domestic layer would be relevant it is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, and the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 commenced 15 March 2026 and is excluded; no Indian provision is cited by number on this question.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: The boundary between a mistake and a violation is not always sharp in practice - a rule-based mistake and a situational violation can look identical from outside, and the difference lies in what the individual believed. The answer describes the categories rather than asserting a diagnostic test. The term 'root cause' is itself contested in the human-factors literature, since a causal chain can always be extended further; the answer resolves this by the ACTIONABILITY test - the analysis stops where the organisation's control begins. And 'proximate cause' carries a distinct meaning in marine insurance, which is named expressly so the two are not conflated.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Eight numbered sections in two equal halves. Limb (a): a three-paragraph regulatory opener, a bulleted principles list, a bulleted steps list, and a prose differentiation section carrying a worked example and a practical test. Limb (b): a prose section on the two models, a prose-plus-bullet section on active failures with an example under each kind, a prose-plus-bullet section on latent failures by category, and a closing bulleted section ending on a single joining sentence.
